name: Aloe vera
summary: A cooling, water-rich plant ingredient with some evidence for healing minor burns. 'Leaf water' is a diluted form that mostly serves as a pleasant base.
what:
Aloe gel from the inner leaf contains polysaccharides (notably acemannan) that hold water and show anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in lab studies. **Aloe barbadensis leaf water** is a watery, diluted form used in place of plain water in a formula; how much active polysaccharide it carries is usually unknown and likely small.

It feels cooling and soothing, which is most of what you notice from an everyday product.

evidence.summary: A 2007 meta-analysis of four trials (371 patients) found aloe shortened healing of first- and second-degree burns by about 9 days, but products and methods varied widely. A systematic review of randomized trials found no evidence that aloe prevents radiation skin reactions. Evidence for sunburn relief and everyday cosmetic benefits is weak.

uses.note: Faster healing in a meta-analysis of small, varied trials.
Feels soothing; controlled evidence of faster recovery is lacking.
Randomized trials reviewed together showed no benefit.
Its sugars act as mild humectants; the rest of the formula matters more.

safety: Allergy is uncommon but occurs; stop if itching or a rash appears.
Don't use raw aloe latex (the yellow sap just under the leaf skin) on skin; it irritates. Cosmetic aloe is processed to remove it.

studies.title: The efficacy of aloe vera used for burn wound healing: a systematic review.
studies.authors: Maenthaisong R, Chaiyakunapruk N, Niruntraporn S, Kongkaew C
studies.finding_summary: Four controlled trials (371 patients) suggested aloe shortened healing of first- and second-degree burns by about 9 days, but differing products and outcomes limit firm conclusions.

studies.title: Aloe vera for preventing radiation-induced skin reactions: a systematic literature review.
studies.authors: Richardson J, Smith JE, McIntyre M, Thomas R, Pilkington K
studies.finding_summary: Five published and two unpublished randomized trials gave no evidence that topical aloe vera prevents or reduces radiation-induced skin reactions in cancer patients.

name: Arbutin (alpha-arbutin)
summary: A hydroquinone-glucose compound that slows pigment production. Gentler than hydroquinone and allowed in cosmetics, with modest, small-study evidence.
what:
Arbutin is hydroquinone joined to a sugar. It inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, more weakly than hydroquinone and without its toxic effect on pigment cells. **Alpha-arbutin** is a manufactured form that is more potent in lab tests; plain (beta-) arbutin occurs naturally in bearberry leaves.

The EU's scientific safety committee considers alpha-arbutin safe up to 2% in face creams and 0.5% in body lotions, provided free hydroquinone stays at trace levels. Arbutin can release hydroquinone as a product ages or on skin, which is why those limits exist.

evidence.summary: Lab studies consistently show it inhibits melanin production. Clinical evidence is a scattering of small trials, often of combination products, showing modest lightening; rigorous placebo-controlled trials of arbutin alone are few.

uses.note: Modest lightening in small studies, often combined with other brighteners.
Some small positive studies; weaker than prescription options.
Gentler, but it can release some hydroquinone; stick to regulated strengths.

safety: Keep to 2% or less on the face and 0.5% on the body; old or heat-exposed products may contain more free hydroquinone.
Contact dermatitis is rare.
It hasn't been studied in pregnancy.

studies.title: Arbutin as a Skin Depigmenting Agent with Antimelanogenic and Antioxidant Properties.
studies.authors: Boo YC
studies.finding_summary: Reviews arbutin's anti-pigment mechanism, clinical studies alone and in combination, and safety: dermatitis is rare, but caution is advised because hydroquinone may be generated during product use.

name: Avobenzone
summary: The main long-wave UVA filter in US sunscreens. Very effective but breaks down in sunlight unless the formula stabilises it.
what:
Avobenzone absorbs UVA1, the long-wave UVA (peak around 357 nm) that penetrates deep into skin and drives photoageing. For decades it was the only organic (non-mineral) filter in US over-the-counter sunscreens with strong UVA1 coverage, so most American 'broad spectrum' chemical sunscreens rely on it.

Its weakness is that it degrades in sunlight. Formulators stabilise it with partners such as octocrylene or bemotrizinol. Paired with octinoxate it is notably unstable. In perfumes it is added in small amounts to protect the product from light, not your skin.

evidence.summary: The only long-term randomised sunscreen trial (Nambour, Australia) used a sunscreen of 8% octinoxate + 2% avobenzone and found fewer squamous-cell cancers, less photoageing and, at 10-year follow-up, fewer melanomas. Avobenzone is absorbed into the blood above the FDA's screening threshold; that threshold triggers further testing and is not a toxicity limit. FDA still lists it as needing more safety data.

uses.note: Its UVA1 coverage is why many US 'broad spectrum' labels are possible; stability depends on the formula.

uses.use: Prevents skin cancer and skin ageing
uses.note: Shown for sunscreen containing it in the Nambour trial, not for avobenzone alone.

uses.use: It is absorbed, so it is unsafe
uses.note: Blood levels of 3-7 ng/mL exceed a screening trigger, not a harm threshold. Lab tests found it not oestrogenic.

avoid_with: octinoxate (unless the formula adds a stabiliser: the pair degrade each other in sunlight)
safety: Contact and photoallergy are uncommon.
It can bind iron and leave orange-brown stains on light fabrics, especially with hard or iron-rich water.
Reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors and after swimming or sweating; a degraded layer protects less.

studies.title: Daily sunscreen application and betacarotene supplementation in prevention of basal-cell and squamous-cell carcinomas of the skin: a randomised controlled trial.
studies.authors: Green A, Williams G, Neale R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 1,621 adults in Nambour, Australia, were randomised to daily or discretionary use of an SPF 15+ sunscreen for 4.5 years. Daily use cut the number of squamous-cell carcinomas by about 39% (rate ratio 0.61) but did not change basal-cell carcinoma, and caused no harm. The trial sunscreen combined octinoxate 8% and avobenzone 2%.

studies.title: Reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use: randomized trial follow-up.
studies.authors: Green AC, Williams GM, Logan V, Strutton GM
studies.finding_summary: Ten years after the Nambour trial ended, the daily-sunscreen group had 11 new melanomas against 22 in the discretionary group (HR 0.50, borderline significance); invasive melanomas fell from 11 to 3. Small numbers, but the only randomised evidence on sunscreen and melanoma.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

studies.title: In vitro and in vivo estrogenicity of UV screens.
studies.authors: Schlumpf M, Cotton B, Conscience M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Oxybenzone, homosalate, octinoxate and two other filters made breast-cancer cells proliferate in a dish; in immature rats, octinoxate and oxybenzone raised uterine weight only at very high oral doses (around 935 and 1,525 mg/kg/day). Avobenzone was inactive. Hazard screening, not evidence of effects at human exposure.

name: Azelaic acid
summary: A prescription treatment for acne, rosacea and dark marks at 15-20%. Cosmetic serums use about 10% or less, where it is much less studied.
what:
Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid made by yeasts that live on skin and found in grains. It kills acne bacteria, normalizes the way pore-lining cells shed, calms inflammation and slows overactive pigment cells. That mix makes it one of the few ingredients that address acne, rosacea bumps and post-acne marks at once.

The proven products are prescription: a 15% gel for rosacea and a 20% cream for acne and pigment. Over-the-counter serums typically contain 10% or less, or list azelaic acid low in the ingredients, so expect gentler and less certain results.

evidence.summary: Prescription 15-20% azelaic acid is backed by multiple randomized trials; the 2024 US acne guideline gives it a conditional recommendation, and a Cochrane review found it probably works about as well as tretinoin but less well than benzoyl peroxide for acne. Evidence at the lower strengths used in cosmetics is sparse.

uses.note: At prescription strength it matched tretinoin and other standard treatments in trials; weaker than benzoyl peroxide.
The 15% gel is an approved rosacea treatment.
20% cream was at least as effective as hydroquinone for melasma in older controlled trials.

uses.use: Low-strength cosmetic versions work the same
uses.note: Serums around 10% or less have little trial data.

works_with: Benzoyl peroxide or retinoids, as a clinician advises
safety: Stinging, burning and itch are common in the first weeks, especially on rosacea-prone skin, and usually fade.
Often suggested as one of the safer acne and pigment options in pregnancy and breastfeeding; confirm with your clinician.
Rarely it lightens skin around the treated area in darker skin tones; report unexpected light patches.

studies.title: Azelaic acid. A review of its pharmacological properties and therapeutic efficacy in acne and hyperpigmentary skin disorders.
studies.authors: Fitton A, Goa KL
studies.finding_summary: Reviews azelaic acid, usually as a 20% cream: in controlled studies it matched tretinoin, benzoyl peroxide, erythromycin and oral tetracycline for acne and was at least as effective as hydroquinone for melasma, with mostly mild, transient irritation.

studies.title: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne.
studies.authors: Liu H, Yu H, Xia J, Liu L, Liu GJ, Sang H, Peinemann F
studies.finding_summary: 49 trials (3,880 people): azelaic acid is probably less effective than benzoyl peroxide and about as effective as tretinoin for acne; evidence for salicylic acid, nicotinamide and alpha-hydroxy acids was low or very low quality, from small head-to-head trials, and no conclusions were reported for zinc or sulphur.

studies.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris.
studies.authors: Reynolds RV, Yeung H, Cheng CE, Cook-Bolden F, Desai SR, Druby KM, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: The American Academy of Dermatology's acne guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline, and conditional (lower-certainty) recommendations for topical salicylic acid, azelaic acid and clascoterone.

name: Bakuchiol
summary: A plant compound sold as a gentle retinol alternative. One small head-to-head trial found it matched 0.5% retinol with less irritation; the evidence is thin.
what:
Bakuchiol comes from the seeds and leaves of the babchi plant (Psoralea corylifolia). It has no structural resemblance to retinoids, but in lab skin models it switched on a similar set of genes, including collagen genes.

The best human study is a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 44 adults: 0.5% bakuchiol twice daily and 0.5% retinol once daily reduced wrinkle area and pigmentation about equally, and the retinol group had more scaling and stinging. That is encouraging, but small, short and without a placebo group.

evidence.summary: One small randomized double-blind comparison with retinol (44 people, 12 weeks, no placebo arm) plus lab work and an uncontrolled case study from the ingredient supplier. Results are promising but unreplicated in large trials; 'as good as retinol' rests on that single trial.

uses.note: Matched 0.5% retinol in one 12-week trial; no large placebo-controlled trials yet.
Improved alongside wrinkles in the same trial.
Caused less scaling and stinging than retinol in the trial.
Often marketed this way, but it has not been studied in pregnancy; 'not a retinoid' is not the same as 'tested safe'.

safety: No pregnancy safety data exist; ask a clinician before relying on it during pregnancy.
Prefer products listing purified bakuchiol over whole babchi seed extracts, which can contain psoralens that make skin more sensitive to sunlight.
Gentler than retinol but not irritation-free; patch test first.

studies.title: Prospective, randomized, double-blind assessment of topical bakuchiol and retinol for facial photoageing.
studies.authors: Dhaliwal S, Rybak I, Ellis SR, Notay M, Trivedi M, Burney W, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 44 adults applied 0.5% bakuchiol cream twice daily or 0.5% retinol cream daily for 12 weeks; both reduced wrinkle surface area and hyperpigmentation with no significant difference, and retinol users reported more scaling and stinging.

studies.title: Bakuchiol: a retinol-like functional compound revealed by gene expression profiling and clinically proven to have anti-aging effects.
studies.authors: Chaudhuri RK, Bojanowski K
studies.finding_summary: From the ingredient supplier: bakuchiol produced a gene-expression profile similar to retinol in a skin model and increased collagen production; a 12-week use study without a control group reported improved lines, pigmentation and firmness.

name: Bemotrizinol
summary: A photostable broad-spectrum filter used outside the US for 25 years. In June 2026 it became the first new US sunscreen active in about two decades (up to 6%).
what:
Bemotrizinol absorbs across UVB and UVA (peaks near 310 and 340 nm), is very stable in sunlight, and stabilises avobenzone when the two are combined. It is a large, oil-soluble molecule (about 630 daltons), which limits how much passes through skin.

It has been allowed in the EU (up to 10%), Australia and Asia since around 2000. In June 2026 the FDA issued a final order adding it to the US sunscreen monograph at up to 6% for adults and children aged 6 months and older, the first addition since the late 1990s.

evidence.summary: Its broad-spectrum absorption and photostability are well documented in formulation testing, and FDA's 2026 review found it safe and effective with low absorption through skin. Long-term clinical outcome trials exist for sunscreens in general, not for this filter specifically.

uses.note: One of the most efficient broad-spectrum filters available.
Keeps avobenzone-containing formulas working through sun exposure.
FDA's review found low skin absorption, consistent with its large molecular size.

safety: Allergy appears rare.
US approval covers adults and children 6 months and older; for younger babies, shade and clothing first.

name: Beta-glucan
summary: A water-binding sugar from oats, yeast or mushrooms. A good humectant and film-former; claims that it beats hyaluronic acid or rebuilds skin lack evidence.
what:
Beta-glucans are long chains of glucose found in oat bran, yeast cell walls and mushrooms. On skin they hold water and form a thin, smoothing film, and lab studies suggest they calm inflammation and support barrier repair.

They are used in soothing toners, ampoules and moisturizers. Large beta-glucan molecules mostly stay on the surface, which suits hydration but limits deeper effects.

evidence.summary: Evidence consists of lab studies, animal work and small manufacturer studies, often with beta-glucan combined with other ingredients. No robust independent trials establish benefits beyond surface hydration.

uses.note: A humectant and film-former, like other skin-conditioning polysaccharides.
Anti-inflammatory in lab work; little human data.
A marketing comparison without independent trials.
Only lab and animal evidence.

safety: Very well tolerated.

name: Betaine salicylate
summary: A salicylic acid compound marketed as a gentler BHA. Chemically related, but with almost no published clinical testing of its own.
what:
Betaine salicylate combines salicylic acid with betaine, a humectant from sugar beets. It is popular in Korean skincare, where it is often described as "4% betaine salicylate equals about 1% salicylic acid" — a comparison from ingredient suppliers, not from trials.

It probably exfoliates like a mild salicylic acid, but whether it performs like the approved acne ingredient hasn't been tested.

evidence.summary: There are no well-designed published trials of betaine salicylate for acne or clogged pores. Its effects are inferred from salicylic acid chemistry.

uses.note: Plausible from its salicylate content; not tested in published trials.
A supplier claim without head-to-head data.

safety: Treat it like salicylic acid: ask a clinician first if you are allergic to aspirin.
Layering it with other acid toners and serums is the usual cause of irritation.

name: Biotin
summary: A B vitamin that helps hair only if you are deficient, which is rare. In shampoo it rinses away before it can do anything useful.
what:
Biotin is a B vitamin the body needs to make keratin. Genuine deficiency (from rare genetic conditions, some medicines, or eating lots of raw egg white) causes hair loss, and correcting it helps.

Most people are not deficient. Added to shampoo or conditioner, biotin sits on the scalp for a minute or two and is rinsed off; there is no evidence it is absorbed in useful amounts or changes hair.

evidence.summary: A systematic review found that every reported case of biotin improving hair or nails involved a deficiency or an underlying disorder, with insufficient evidence for healthy people. There are no controlled trials of topical biotin in shampoo.

uses.note: No trials of topical biotin; rinse-off contact is brief.

uses.use: Treats hair loss from biotin deficiency
uses.note: True for oral biotin when a deficiency is confirmed, which is uncommon.
Pattern hair loss is hormonal and genetic; biotin does not address it.

typical: Small amounts in shampoos and conditioners (rarely disclosed)
safety: Topical biotin is harmless.
If you also take high-dose biotin supplements, tell your clinician before blood tests: biotin can distort results of some thyroid, hormone and heart (troponin) tests.
New or sudden hair loss deserves a medical check (thyroid, iron, medications, scalp conditions) rather than a biotin product.

studies.title: A Review of the Use of Biotin for Hair Loss.
studies.authors: Patel DP, Swink SM, Castelo-Soccio L
studies.finding_summary: All 18 reported cases where biotin improved hair or nails involved an underlying disorder or deficiency; there was no sufficient evidence for biotin in healthy people.

name: Bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate
summary: The patented 'bond-building' active in popular repair treatments. Hair does look and feel better; the claim that it rejoins broken bonds inside hair is unproven.
what:
Bleaching and colouring break disulfide bonds, the cross-links that give hair strength. This ingredient, a maleate salt, is claimed to react with the broken ends and link them back together, and it is sold as a pre-treatment during bleaching and as an at-home mask, shampoo and conditioner.

Independent lab analysis of bleached hair treated with maleate-type repair agents found a smoother, more intact-looking surface but no increase in disulfide bonds and no direct sign of the claimed cross-linking.

evidence.summary: Evidence consists mainly of manufacturer lab testing (breakage and strength measurements). An independent spectroscopy study of maleate-type repair agents found cosmetic surface improvement but no evidence of rebuilt bonds. There are no controlled trials on real-world breakage.

uses.use: Hair feels smoother and stronger after bleaching
uses.note: Surface improvement is seen in the lab; whether breakage falls in real use has not been independently tested.
Not shown in independent structural analysis.

uses.use: Makes bleaching safe for any hair
uses.note: It may reduce damage; over-processed hair still breaks.

typical: Concentration not usually disclosed; highest in salon pre-treatments and masks
safety: Generally well tolerated.
Bleaching chemicals are the main risk to hair and scalp; a bond treatment does not make repeated heavy bleaching safe. Stop if the scalp burns.

studies.title: Structural investigation on damaged hair keratin treated with alpha,beta-unsaturated Michael acceptors used as repairing agents.
studies.authors: Di Foggia M, Boga C, Micheletti G, Nocentini B, Taddei P
studies.finding_summary: On bleached hair, maleate- and shikimic-acid-based repair agents changed the cuticle and cortex and made the surface smoother, but none increased disulfide bonds in the cortex, and nothing directly showed the claimed cross-linking reaction.

name: Bisabolol
summary: The main calming compound in chamomile oil, added to sensitive-skin, shaving and after-sun products. Anti-inflammatory in lab work; little human trial data.
what:
Alpha-bisabolol is a fragrant alcohol that makes up much of German chamomile essential oil; it is also obtained from the candeia tree or made synthetically. It reduces inflammation and irritation in lab and animal models and can help other ingredients penetrate skin.

It is usually a supporting ingredient in products for sensitive skin, redness, shaving and after-sun, typically below 1%.

evidence.summary: Evidence is mainly from cell and animal studies plus manufacturer testing of blends. Independent controlled trials of bisabolol alone on human skin conditions are scarce.

uses.note: Anti-inflammatory in lab studies; not well tested alone in people.
Widely used for this; no good trials of bisabolol itself.

safety: Generally low in irritation and allergy, but people with daisy-family (Compositae) allergy should patch test.

name: Bisoctrizole
summary: A particle-form organic filter covering UVB through long-wave UVA. Photostable and barely absorbed; allowed in the EU at 10% but not approved in the US.
what:
Bisoctrizole is an organic filter made as microfine particles dispersed in the water phase, so, like the mineral filters, it both absorbs and scatters UV. It covers UVB through UVA1 (peaks near 305 and 360 nm) and is very photostable.

It is permitted in the EU (up to 10%, including a nano form, which is not allowed in sprays), Australia and much of Asia. It is not an approved sunscreen active in the US, so products containing it here are generally imported formulas.

evidence.summary: Its broad-spectrum absorption and stability are established in formulation and SPF/UVA testing. Toxicology reviews found no genotoxicity or reproductive toxicity and low absorption, with a wide margin of safety at 10%. Clinical outcome trials exist for sunscreens in general, not for this filter specifically.

uses.note: One of the few single filters reaching long-wave UVA.
Large molecule in particle form; dermal absorption is low in the safety data.

typical: Up to 10% (EU); not permitted as a US sunscreen active
safety: Allergy is rare; most reported cases traced to decyl glucoside, the surfactant used to disperse the particles, rather than to the filter itself. If you react, ask for patch testing to both.
Imported sunscreens are not reviewed by the FDA; buy from sources that sell genuine stock.

studies.title: Safety assessment of methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol, a UV filter in cosmetics.
studies.authors: Kim M, Kim SB, Lee JD, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Reviewing animal and lab data, the filter showed no genotoxicity, no reproductive or developmental effects up to 1,000 mg/kg/day, and no skin sensitisation at 30%. The calculated margin of safety exceeded 100 at 10% use in all cosmetics.

name: Caffeine
summary: Stimulates hair follicles in a dish and reaches them from a shampoo, but proof that caffeine products slow hair loss in people is thin. Eye-cream claims are weaker still.
what:
In **hair products**, caffeine is meant to counter the hormone-driven shrinking of follicles in pattern hair loss. It does reach follicles quickly from a shampoo, and it stimulates growth in follicles kept alive in a dish.

In **eye creams and serums**, caffeine is marketed to reduce puffiness and dark circles by narrowing blood vessels. That is plausible, but there is little trial evidence and any effect is short-lived.

evidence.summary: Lab studies show caffeine stimulates human hair follicles in culture, and a pharmacokinetic study shows it enters follicles within 2 minutes of shampooing. The only sizeable clinical trial (210 men) was open-label, had no placebo arm, and found a 0.2% leave-on caffeine liquid 'non-inferior' to 5% minoxidil on a growing-hair ratio, not hair count. No placebo-controlled trial shows caffeine shampoo reduces hair loss.

uses.note: One open-label trial without placebo; needs independent confirmation.
Caffeine reaches follicles, but no trial shows a benefit from rinse-off use.
Plausible short-term vasoconstriction; little clinical evidence.
Circles caused by pigment or thin skin won't respond.
Promotes fat breakdown in lab studies; no convincing trials of visible change.

typical: About 0.2-1% in hair tonics and shampoos; up to a few percent in eye products
safety: Topical caffeine is generally well tolerated; the amount absorbed is small.
For progressing pattern hair loss, the proven options are minoxidil and (for men) finasteride; see a clinician rather than relying on caffeine products.
Sudden, patchy or rapid hair loss needs medical assessment.

studies.title: Effect of caffeine and testosterone on the proliferation of human hair follicles in vitro.
studies.authors: Fischer TW, Hipler UC, Elsner P
studies.finding_summary: In hair follicles taken from men with pattern hair loss and grown in a dish, caffeine at 0.001-0.005% counteracted testosterone's growth suppression and stimulated hair shaft growth on its own.

studies.title: Follicular penetration of topically applied caffeine via a shampoo formulation.
studies.authors: Otberg N, Teichmann A, Rasuljev U, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Caffeine from a shampoo left on for 2 minutes reached the blood, entering faster via hair follicles than through the skin surface. Shows delivery is possible, not that it grows hair.

studies.title: An Open-Label Randomized Multicenter Study Assessing the Noninferiority of a Caffeine-Based Topical Liquid 0.2% versus Minoxidil 5% Solution in Male Androgenetic Alopecia.
studies.authors: Dhurat R, Chitallia J, May TW, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 210 men used a 0.2% caffeine leave-on liquid or 5% minoxidil for 6 months; the share of growing-phase hairs rose by 10.6% and 11.7% respectively, and caffeine was judged non-inferior. Open-label, no placebo, and a trichogram rather than hair-count endpoint.

studies.title: Caffeine's mechanisms of action and its cosmetic use.
studies.authors: Herman A, Herman AP
studies.finding_summary: Reviews caffeine's skin penetration and cosmetic uses, noting topical products usually contain about 3%: fat breakdown in anti-cellulite products, antioxidant and UV-protective effects, increased microcirculation and hair-growth stimulation, largely from lab data.

name: Calcium carbonate
summary: Chalk used as a toothpaste abrasive, usually paired with sodium monofluorophosphate. Cleans well; claims that it 'remineralises' teeth are mostly theory.
what:
Calcium carbonate is a mild-to-moderate abrasive that has been used in toothpaste for over a century. Because its calcium would bind free fluoride, chalk pastes use sodium monofluorophosphate rather than sodium fluoride.

Manufacturers suggest the chalk particles also raise calcium in plaque and neutralise acid, which in theory could help fluoride work. That is plausible, but it has not been shown to prevent more decay than silica pastes with the same fluoride.

evidence.summary: Calcium carbonate-SMFP toothpastes prevent decay in clinical trials, with the effect attributed to the fluoride. The added calcium/acid-neutralising benefit is mechanistic and comes largely from industry-authored reviews.

uses.note: A proven abrasive.
Plausible mechanism; no trials showing benefit beyond the fluoride it is paired with.

typical: Often a large share of chalk-based pastes (tens of percent)
avoid_with: sodium fluoride in the same paste (the calcium inactivates it)
safety: Generally safe; if you have sensitive or exposed roots, prefer a low-abrasion paste.

studies.title: The anti-caries efficacy of calcium carbonate-based fluoride toothpastes.
studies.authors: Lynch RJ, ten Cate JM
studies.finding_summary: Sodium monofluorophosphate in calcium carbonate toothpastes is an effective anti-caries combination in numerous clinical trials; the authors propose that calcium carbonate may add benefit by raising plaque calcium and neutralising acid, which is mechanistic and not separately proven.

name: Calendula (marigold) extract
summary: A marigold extract in balms and body care for soothing and minor skin damage. Radiotherapy trials conflict: one large trial favoured it, another found no difference.
what:
Calendula flowers contain triterpenes, flavonoids and carotenoids with anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in lab and animal studies. It is a staple of baby balms, nappy creams and body lotions.

The most rigorous human tests come from breast cancer radiotherapy. A 254-patient trial found fewer moderate-to-severe skin reactions with a calendula ointment than with a standard trolamine cream (41% vs 63%); a later 420-patient blinded trial found a calendula cream no better than a simple aqueous cream.

evidence.summary: Two randomized trials in radiotherapy disagree, and both used medicinal-strength preparations rather than the low levels in most body products. Other evidence is small wound and nappy-rash studies plus lab work.

uses.note: One large trial favoured calendula over trolamine; a larger blinded trial found no difference from plain aqueous cream.
Plausible from lab work; not well tested at cosmetic levels.
Small studies only.

safety: A daisy-family (Compositae) plant: can trigger allergy in people sensitive to ragweed, chamomile or arnica.
During radiotherapy, use only skin products your treatment team approves.

studies.title: Phase III randomized trial of Calendula officinalis compared with trolamine for the prevention of acute dermatitis during irradiation for breast cancer.
studies.authors: Pommier P, Gomez F, Sunyach MP, D'Hombres A, Carrie C, Montbarbon X
studies.finding_summary: 254 women having breast radiotherapy were randomized to calendula ointment or trolamine cream; grade 2 or worse dermatitis occurred in 41% versus 63%, with less pain and fewer treatment interruptions on calendula.

studies.title: No differences between Calendula cream and aqueous cream in the prevention of acute radiation skin reactions--results from a randomised blinded trial.
studies.authors: Sharp L, Finnilä K, Johansson H, Abrahamsson M, Hatschek T, Bergenmar M
studies.finding_summary: Among 411 analysed breast cancer patients, a calendula cream was no better than a plain aqueous cream at preventing radiation skin reactions (23% vs 19%), and patient-reported symptoms did not differ.

name: Centella asiatica (cica)
summary: 'Cica', the Korean-skincare staple. Its triterpenes aid wound healing in studies; for everyday redness and barrier repair the evidence is small but encouraging.
what:
Centella asiatica (gotu kola) is a creeping plant long used on wounds. Its active compounds are four triterpenes — **madecassoside, asiaticoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid** — which in lab and animal work increase collagen production and dampen inflammation. Products list either the whole extract or one of these purified compounds.

Marketed as 'cica', it is sold for irritated, red or over-exfoliated skin and for barrier repair. Those uses fit its lab profile, but most human studies test it in combination with other actives.

evidence.summary: Wound and scar studies (often older and small) and lab work support its activity. Cosmetic trials mostly test mixtures — a 6-month double-blind study of 5% vitamin C plus 0.1% madecassoside improved wrinkles and firmness, but can't isolate centella's share. Good placebo-controlled trials of centella alone for redness or sensitivity are lacking.

uses.note: Anti-inflammatory in lab work; human evidence mostly from combination products.

uses.use: Barrier repair after procedures or over-exfoliation
uses.note: Plausible and widely used; few controlled trials.
Supported by older clinical and lab work; results vary by preparation.
Only tested alongside vitamin C.

safety: Well tolerated; allergic contact dermatitis is reported but uncommon.
'Soothing' products can still contain fragrance or essential oils — check the full ingredient list.

studies.title: Centella asiatica in cosmetology.
studies.authors: Bylka W, Znajdek-Awiżeń P, Studzińska-Sroka E, Brzezińska M
studies.finding_summary: Reviews centella's triterpenes (asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic and madecassic acids), their pro-collagen and anti-inflammatory actions, and their use for wounds, scars, burns, photoaging, cellulite and stretch marks.

studies.title: Clinical, biometric and structural evaluation of the long-term effects of a topical treatment with ascorbic acid and madecassoside in photoaged human skin.
studies.authors: Haftek M, Mac-Mary S, Le Bitoux MA, Creidi P, Seité S, Rougier A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 20 women with photoaged skin used 5% vitamin C with 0.1% madecassoside for 6 months in a randomized double-blind study; wrinkles, firmness, roughness and hydration improved, with a better elastic fibre network on biopsy. The design can't separate the two ingredients.

name: Cetylpyridinium chloride
summary: An antiseptic in many alcohol-free mouthwashes. Adds a small extra reduction in plaque and gum inflammation to brushing; can stain teeth.
what:
Cetylpyridinium chloride is a positively charged antiseptic that disrupts bacterial membranes and clings to mouth surfaces for a few hours. It is the main active in many alcohol-free rinses, typically at 0.05-0.1%.

Because it is positively charged, the foaming agent in most toothpastes (sodium lauryl sulfate) can partly neutralise it. Using the rinse at a different time from brushing avoids this.

evidence.summary: Systematic reviews find a small but significant added benefit for plaque and gingivitis when CPC rinses are used alongside brushing; a network meta-analysis ranked rinses above 0.05% CPC among the more effective. Results vary with the formula. For bad breath, a Cochrane review found only low-certainty evidence of modest improvement.

uses.note: Small extra benefit; formulation matters.
Short-term improvement with low-certainty evidence.
Rinses are an add-on to mechanical cleaning.

avoid_with: rinsing straight after brushing with a sodium lauryl sulfate toothpaste (may reduce effect; use at a separate time)
safety: Can cause brown surface staining on teeth and a temporary change in taste.
Do not swallow; follow the age limit on the label, as young children cannot reliably spit.
Bleeding gums that persist need a dental assessment, not just a rinse.

studies.title: The effect of cetylpyridinium chloride-containing mouth rinses as adjuncts to toothbrushing on plaque and parameters of gingival inflammation: a systematic review.
studies.authors: Haps S, Slot DE, Berchier CE, Van der Weijden GA
studies.finding_summary: Eight studies: CPC rinses used alongside brushing gave a small but significant extra reduction in plaque and gum inflammation.

studies.title: Efficacy of adjunctive anti-plaque chemical agents in managing gingivitis: A systematic review and network meta-analyses.
studies.authors: Figuero E, Herrera D, Tobias A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 53 six-month trials. Among rinses, essential oils, chlorhexidine (0.10% or more) and cetylpyridinium chloride (above 0.05%) had the largest effects on gingivitis, with essential oils ranking highest; active toothpastes differed little from each other, with baking soda among the weakest.

studies.title: Interventions for managing halitosis.
studies.authors: Kumbargere Nagraj S, Eachempati P, Uma E, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 44 mostly short trials: evidence for every bad-breath intervention was low to very low certainty. Brushing plus a CPC rinse modestly improved examiner odour scores (low certainty); no product could be shown to be better than another.

name: Chamomile extract
summary: A traditional soothing flower extract in skin and hair products. Mildly anti-inflammatory in lab work, little trial evidence, and an allergen for daisy-family allergy.
what:
Chamomile flower extract carries flavonoids such as apigenin, plus bisabolol and chamazulene from the essential oil, which account for its anti-inflammatory effect in lab studies. It is used in calming skincare, baby products and 'blonde-brightening' shampoos, which claim to enhance golden tones.

Chamomile belongs to the daisy (Compositae) family, whose plants are a recognized cause of allergic contact dermatitis.

evidence.summary: Reviews describe long traditional use and lab anti-inflammatory activity; controlled trials of chamomile skin products are few, small and usually of branded combination creams. There is no evidence it lightens or brightens hair.

uses.note: Plausible from lab work; few controlled trials.
No published evidence at the levels used in shampoos.

safety: People allergic to ragweed, daisies, arnica or other Compositae plants can react; in one study, 8 of 12 chamomile-sensitive patients reacted to chamomile teas, creams, ointments or oil.
Rarely, chamomile causes contact hives (urticaria).

studies.title: Chamomile: A herbal medicine of the past with bright future.
studies.authors: Srivastava JK, Shankar E, Gupta S
studies.finding_summary: Reviews the chemistry of German and Roman chamomile (terpenoids, flavonoids) and its traditional and investigated medicinal uses, including for inflammation and wounds, and its use in cosmetics and aromatherapy.

studies.title: Cosmetics and herbal remedies with Compositae plant extracts - are they tolerated by Compositae-allergic patients?
studies.authors: Paulsen E, Chistensen LP, Andersen KE
studies.finding_summary: 8 of 12 chamomile-sensitive patients reacted to chamomile-containing tea, creams, ointments or oil; the authors advise people with Compositae allergy to avoid Compositae-containing cosmetics and remedies.

name: Collagen (topical)
summary: In creams, collagen is a moisturizer. The molecule is far too large to enter skin, so it cannot replace or rebuild your own collagen.
what:
Collagen is the main structural protein of the dermis. In skincare it is usually animal- or fish-derived collagen or smaller hydrolyzed fragments. An intact collagen molecule weighs around 300,000 daltons, while molecules much above 500 daltons don't get through the skin's outer layer, so collagen stays on the surface.

There it works as a **humectant and film-former**: it holds water and leaves skin feeling smoother and plumper for a while. That is real but temporary, and it's the same job glycerin or hyaluronic acid does. 'Collagen' serums that claim to boost your own collagen rely on other actives, such as retinoids, vitamin C or peptides, for any effect. Oral collagen supplements are a separate question with their own evidence.

evidence.summary: No credible evidence shows that collagen applied to skin increases skin collagen or firmness; the size limit on skin penetration is basic physiology. Its moisturizing effect is real but modest and short-lived.

uses.note: Far too large to penetrate; your collagen is made by fibroblasts deep in the dermis.
Holds water on the surface, like other humectants.
Any plumping is temporary surface hydration.

safety: Well tolerated. Most cosmetic collagen is animal- or fish-derived, which matters if you avoid animal products.

studies.title: The 500 Dalton rule for the skin penetration of chemical compounds and drugs.
studies.authors: Bos JD, Meinardi MM
studies.finding_summary: Argues that a compound must weigh under about 500 daltons to pass through the skin's outer layer, based on the size of known contact allergens and of the drugs that work topically or through transdermal patches.

name: Colloidal oatmeal
summary: Finely ground oats: an FDA-recognized skin protectant for itch and minor irritation, with small eczema trials. Kind to most skin, but can sensitize infants.
what:
Colloidal oatmeal is whole oat kernel ground very fine so it disperses in water. Its starches and beta-glucan form a protective, water-holding film; avenanthramides and other phenols calm inflammation and itch; saponins cleanse gently. In the US it is one of the few botanical ingredients approved as an over-the-counter **skin protectant**, for temporary relief of itch and irritation from rashes, eczema, poison ivy and insect bites.

Labels list it as 'colloidal oatmeal' when it is the regulated active and often as 'Avena sativa kernel flour' when used as a cosmetic ingredient — essentially the same material, though only the drug version must meet the pharmacopeia standard.

evidence.summary: The FDA recognizes it as safe and effective as a skin protectant. Small trials, mostly from one manufacturer and without placebo arms, show 1% colloidal oatmeal creams improve eczema severity, itch, dryness and barrier measures within days to two weeks, and lab work explains the anti-inflammatory effect.

uses.note: An FDA-monograph skin protectant for temporary relief of minor irritation and itch.
Two small single-arm studies of a 1% cream showed less itch and better eczema scores; a good moisturizer, not a replacement for prescribed treatment in flares.

uses.use: Soothing baths for rashes and bites
uses.note: Covered by the same skin-protectant approval.

safety: Infants and young children with eczema can become sensitized to oat proteins; in one clinic study, 32% of oat-cream users had positive oat patch tests versus none of the non-users. Consider oat-free emollients for babies with eczema.
Stop if a product causes itching or hives.

studies.title: Colloidal oatmeal: history, chemistry and clinical properties.
studies.authors: Kurtz ES, Wallo W
studies.finding_summary: Reviews colloidal oatmeal's chemistry and its regulation as an FDA-monograph skin protectant: starches and beta-glucan protect and hold water, phenols are antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, and saponins cleanse. Written by manufacturer scientists.

studies.title: Anti-inflammatory activities of colloidal oatmeal (Avena sativa) contribute to the effectiveness of oats in treatment of itch associated with dry, irritated skin.
studies.authors: Reynertson KA, Garay M, Nebus J, Chon S, Kaur S, Mahmood K, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Colloidal oatmeal extracts reduced inflammatory signals in lab tests, and in an investigator-blinded study of 29 women with itchy, dry lower legs, a colloidal oatmeal lotion improved dryness, scaling, roughness and itch.

studies.title: A 1% Colloidal Oatmeal Cream Alone is Effective in Reducing Symptoms of Mild to Moderate Atopic Dermatitis: Results from Two Clinical Studies.
studies.authors: Lisante TA, Nunez C, Zhang P, Mathes BM
studies.finding_summary: In two single-arm studies (29 and 30 people) with mild to moderate eczema, a 1% colloidal oatmeal cream used for 14 days improved eczema severity, itch, hydration and water loss, with few adverse events.

studies.title: Oat sensitization in children with atopic dermatitis: prevalence, risks and associated factors.
studies.authors: Boussault P, Léauté-Labrèze C, Saubusse E, Maurice-Tison S, Perromat M, Roul S, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Of 302 children with eczema referred for allergy testing, 14.6% had positive oat patch tests and 19.2% positive prick tests; 32% of oat-cream users were patch-test positive versus 0% of non-users. The authors suggest avoiding oat-protein products in infants with eczema.

name: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB)
summary: A photostable long-wave UVA filter used in Europe and Asia as an alternative to avobenzone. Not approved in the US; a phthalate impurity in some batches is now capped in the EU.
what:
DHHB absorbs UVA1 (peak around 354 nm), the same band as avobenzone, but it stays stable in sunlight. It is common in European and Asian sunscreens and is permitted in the EU up to 10%; it is not an approved sunscreen active in the US.

In 2024 German biomonitoring found a banned reproductive-toxic phthalate (di-n-hexyl phthalate, DnHexP) turning up in people's urine, traced in part to contaminated DHHB. In 2025 the EU's safety committee confirmed DHHB is safe up to 10% provided the impurity stays below 260 ppm, with under 1 ppm as the target.

evidence.summary: UVA1 absorption and photostability are well established, and toxicology reviews find low absorption (around 0.15%), no genotoxicity and a large margin of safety at 10%. The phthalate issue is a manufacturing impurity, not a property of DHHB itself, and is now limited in the EU.

uses.note: A stable alternative to avobenzone for UVA1 coverage.
Dermal absorption is low in the safety data.

typical: Up to 10% (EU); not permitted as a US sunscreen active
safety: The phthalate impurity problem is a supply-chain issue: products from established EU-market manufacturers must now meet the impurity limit.
Allergy appears rare.

studies.title: Risk assessment of diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB) as a UV filter in cosmetics.
studies.authors: Lee JD, Kim HY, Lee JY, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Available data show low acute toxicity, no genotoxicity and minimal irritation or sensitisation. With 0.15% dermal absorption and daily sunscreen use at 10%, the margin of safety was about 4,700, well above the usual threshold of 100.

studies.title: Assessing the exposure to the UV filter DHHB in urine samples from the German Environmental Specimen Bank (2000-2021): Evaluating the impact of a potential impurity of di-n-hexyl phthalate in DHHB.
studies.authors: Scherer M, Scherer G, Riedel K, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 250 archived German urine samples, DHHB metabolites first appeared in 2012; intake was far below the no-effect level. Separately, oral-dosing data showed that a phthalate impurity (DnHexP, a reproductive toxicant) in some DHHB batches reaches users, which the authors say warrants reassessment.

name: Eucalyptus oil
summary: A fresh, cooling scent in body washes, lotions and balms. It adds fragrance and a tingle, not a skin benefit, and is toxic if swallowed.
what: Eucalyptus oil is mostly 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol), which gives the familiar medicinal, cooling smell. In body care it is a fragrance ingredient, often paired with mint for a tingling feel. Any 'clearing' sensation from a eucalyptus body wash comes from the scent.

evidence.summary: No trials show eucalyptus oil in personal-care products benefits skin. Its effects are sensory: scent and a mild cooling feeling.

uses.note: A real sensory effect, and the reason it's used.
No trials in personal-care products.

safety: As an essential-oil fragrance it can irritate or cause allergy, especially on shaved or broken skin.
Keep bottles of eucalyptus oil away from children; swallowing small amounts can cause serious poisoning.
Don't apply eucalyptus products near the nose or face of babies and young children.

name: Ferments and ferment lysates
summary: Liquids left after yeast or bacteria ferment, sold as essences and 'probiotic' skincare. Hydrating; beyond that, evidence is small and mostly manufacturer-run.
what:
Ferment filtrates are the strained liquid from growing yeasts such as galactomyces or saccharomyces; lysates are broken-open, non-living bacteria such as bifida or lactobacillus. They contain amino acids, sugars, organic acids, vitamins and peptides that act as humectants and may support the skin barrier.

'Probiotic' skincare is a misnomer: these products don't contain live microbes. Whether lysates usefully shift the skin's own microbes is an open research question.

evidence.summary: Evidence comes mainly from lab studies and trials run by the companies that sell these ingredients. A double-blind trial of a 10% bifida lysate cream in 66 women with reactive skin found less sensitivity and dryness after two months. A 12-month study of galactomyces products reported fewer wrinkles and spots but had no control group and was run by the manufacturer.

uses.note: Humectant contents; improvements reported mostly in industry studies.
One manufacturer-run placebo-controlled trial found less sensitivity.
The main galactomyces study had no control group.

uses.use: Probiotic balancing of the skin microbiome
uses.note: No live microbes are present, and microbiome benefits aren't shown.

safety: Generally well tolerated.

studies.title: Bifidobacterium longum lysate, a new ingredient for reactive skin.
studies.authors: Guéniche A, Bastien P, Ovigne JM, Kermici M, Courchay G, Chevalier V, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 66 women with reactive skin used a cream with 10% bifida lysate or a control cream twice daily for 2 months; the lysate group had less skin sensitivity, better barrier resistance and less dryness. Run by a cosmetics company.

studies.title: Significant Reversal of Facial Wrinkle, Pigmented Spot and Roughness by Daily Application of Galactomyces Ferment Filtrate-Containing Skin Products for 12 Months-An 11-Year Longitudinal Skin Aging Rejuvenation Study.
studies.authors: Miyamoto K, Inoue Y, Yan X, Yagi S, Suda S, Furue M
studies.finding_summary: 86 women used galactomyces ferment filtrate products twice daily for 12 months; hydration rose and wrinkle, spot and roughness measures improved from their 11-year decline. No control group; the authors were employees of or consultants to the manufacturer.

name: Ferulic acid
summary: A plant antioxidant used mainly to stabilize vitamins C and E. In that trio it doubled protection against UV damage in lab skin tests.
what:
Ferulic acid is a polyphenol found in bran, seeds and many plants. Its best-known role in skincare is as a helper: added to a serum of 15% L-ascorbic acid and 1% vitamin E, it slowed the vitamin C from breaking down and doubled the formula's protection against UV-induced redness and sunburn cells, from about 4-fold to 8-fold.

On its own it has antioxidant and mild pigment-lightening activity in lab studies, but few human trials test it alone.

evidence.summary: The key evidence is one lab-and-skin study from a single research group showing ferulic acid stabilized and strengthened a vitamin C + E serum. Evidence for ferulic acid alone on wrinkles or spots in people is sparse; reviews rely mainly on lab work.

uses.use: Stabilizing vitamin C and E serums
uses.note: Improved the chemical stability of a 15% vitamin C + 1% vitamin E solution.
In the vitamin C + E combination it doubled UV protection on lab measures; it still provides no SPF.
Inhibits pigment production in lab studies; not tested well in people.

safety: Low irritation on its own; the stinging people notice usually comes from the acidic vitamin C it is paired with.

studies.title: Ferulic acid stabilizes a solution of vitamins C and E and doubles its photoprotection of skin.
studies.authors: Lin FH, Lin JY, Gupta RD, Tournas JA, Burch JA, Selim MA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Adding ferulic acid to a 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol solution improved its chemical stability and doubled its protection of skin against solar-simulated UV (from about 4-fold to about 8-fold), measured by redness and sunburn cells; thymine dimer formation was also reduced.

studies.title: Antioxidant Properties of Ferulic Acid and Its Possible Application.
studies.authors: Zduńska K, Dana A, Kolodziejczak A, Rotsztejn H
studies.finding_summary: Reviews ferulic acid's antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-pigment properties and its use as a photoprotective and brightening ingredient, noting that its tendency to oxidize limits formulation.

name: Flaxseed extract
summary: A slippery seed mucilage used for light hold and curl definition, and as a moisturising film. No health effects.
what: Soaking or extracting flaxseed releases a gel (mucilage) that forms a flexible film on hair. It gives soft hold and helps curls clump together, and in skin products it acts as a light humectant.

evidence.summary: There is no clinical evidence for health benefits of topical flaxseed extract. Its effects are cosmetic (hold, softness).

uses.note: A physical film-forming effect.
No evidence.

typical: Small amounts in styling products; not usually disclosed
safety: Very low risk; rare allergy in people allergic to flaxseed.

name: Gluconolactone (PHA)
summary: A polyhydroxy acid: a large, gentle exfoliant that also holds water. Suits skin that can't tolerate glycolic acid; the evidence base is small.
what:
Gluconolactone is a polyhydroxy acid (PHA) derived from glucose. Its larger molecule enters skin slowly, so it exfoliates more gently than glycolic acid, and its many hydroxyl groups make it a humectant. It is also an antioxidant.

PHAs are pitched for sensitive or rosacea-prone skin and for pairing with retinoids. The rationale is sound; the supporting studies are few and small.

evidence.summary: A double-blind trial in 150 people found 14% gluconolactone lotion and 5% benzoyl peroxide both reduced acne lesions versus vehicle, with fewer side effects from gluconolactone. Other reports describe smoothing and anti-aging benefits and good tolerance on sensitive skin, but independent replication is limited.

uses.note: Reported to be well tolerated on rosacea- and eczema-prone skin; few controlled comparisons.
One 1992 trial found benefit versus vehicle with fewer side effects than benzoyl peroxide; little follow-up since.
A humectant: it binds water in the outer layer.

safety: Mild, but can still sting on broken or freshly exfoliated skin.
Use sunscreen, as with any exfoliant.

studies.title: A comparative study of gluconolactone versus benzoyl peroxide in the treatment of acne.
studies.authors: Hunt MJ, Barnetson RS
studies.finding_summary: In a double-blind trial of 150 people with mild to moderate acne, 14% gluconolactone and 5% benzoyl peroxide both reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesions versus vehicle; gluconolactone caused fewer side effects.

studies.title: The use of polyhydroxy acids (PHAs) in photoaged skin.
studies.authors: Grimes PE, Green BA, Wildnauer RH, Edison BL
studies.finding_summary: Reviews polyhydroxy acids such as gluconolactone, reporting AHA-like smoothing and anti-aging effects with less stinging, added humectant properties, and compatibility with sensitive skin, rosacea and use after procedures.

name: Glutathione
summary: The body's main internal antioxidant, sold as a skin brightener. Topical evidence is one small company-run trial; IV 'whitening' drips are unproven and risky.
what:
Glutathione is a three-amino-acid peptide every cell makes to neutralize oxidants. It also shifts pigment production away from dark eumelanin, which is behind its reputation as a skin-lightening ingredient.

In skincare it is unstable and oxidizes easily, and how much reaches pigment cells is unclear. In a 10-week split-face trial by an ingredient maker, a 2% oxidized-glutathione lotion lowered the skin's melanin index versus placebo in 30 women. Reviews call the overall evidence thin and the marketing ahead of it.

evidence.summary: One randomized, placebo-controlled topical trial (30 women, run by the ingredient's manufacturer) and a few small oral trials support modest lightening. Intravenous glutathione for skin lightening has no proof of efficacy and has drawn regulatory safety warnings. How long any effect lasts is unknown.

uses.note: One small placebo-controlled trial found a lower melanin index at 10 weeks; not independently replicated.
Plausible from its biology, but not shown for topical products.
No evidence it works, and adverse effects have prompted a public warning from a national drug regulator.

safety: Topical glutathione is generally well tolerated.
Avoid intravenous glutathione drips for skin lightening: no proven benefit and reported serious adverse effects.

studies.title: Skin-whitening and skin-condition-improving effects of topical oxidized glutathione: a double-blind and placebo-controlled clinical trial in healthy women.
studies.authors: Watanabe F, Hashizume E, Chan GP, Kamimura A
studies.finding_summary: 30 women applied 2% oxidized glutathione lotion to one side of the face and placebo to the other for 10 weeks; the melanin index fell significantly more on the glutathione side, which also gained hydration and smoothness. Conducted by the ingredient's manufacturer.

studies.title: Glutathione as a skin whitening agent: Facts, myths, evidence and controversies.
studies.authors: Sonthalia S, Daulatabad D, Sarkar R
studies.journal: Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology
studies.finding_summary: Three small randomized trials support modest lightening from topical and oral glutathione; intravenous use has no evidence of efficacy and led the Philippine drug regulator to issue a public warning. Duration and durability of effect are unknown.

name: Glycolic acid
summary: The smallest, most penetrating AHA. At 5-10% it smooths texture and evens tone over months, but raises sunburn risk while you use it.
what:
Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA). It loosens the bonds between dead cells in the outer layer so they shed faster, which smooths and brightens skin; with long use at higher strengths it also thickens the epidermis and increases dermal collagen.

Strength depends on both percentage and **pH**: the lower the pH, the more free acid and the stronger (and more irritating) the effect. The US cosmetic ingredient safety panel considers AHAs safe in consumer products up to 10% at pH 3.5 or higher; 20-70% peels belong in a clinic.

evidence.summary: A 22-week double-blind trial in 74 women found 8% glycolic acid cream improved overall photodamage more than vehicle (76% vs 40% improved by at least one grade), and a 25% lotion thickened skin and raised collagen density in a biopsy study. Effects at consumer strengths are modest. A controlled study found 10% glycolic acid for 4 weeks made skin burn more easily in UV light.

uses.note: Speeds shedding of dead surface cells; visible smoothing within weeks.
Modest improvement at 8% over about 5 months; larger effects at clinic peel strengths.
Helps as an add-on and in peels; weaker alone than dedicated pigment treatments, and irritation can darken brown skin.
Peels help acne in small trials; salicylic acid gets into oily pores better.

avoid_with: Retinoids, other acids or benzoyl peroxide in the same session if your skin is sensitive
Waxing, laser or professional peels in the same week
safety: Use sunscreen daily while using it and for a week after stopping: in a controlled study, 10% glycolic acid made skin burn more easily, an effect that faded within a week.
Stinging, redness and peeling are common; stop if skin burns or cracks. Darker skin tones risk dark marks from irritation.
Don't use on broken, sunburned or eczema-flared skin.
Low-strength products are generally considered acceptable in pregnancy because little is absorbed.

studies.title: Topical 8% glycolic acid and 8% L-lactic acid creams for the treatment of photodamaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled clinical trial.
studies.authors: Stiller MJ, Bartolone J, Stern R, Smith S, Kollias N, Gillies R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 74 women with photodamaged skin used 8% glycolic acid, 8% L-lactic acid or vehicle cream twice daily for 22 weeks; at least one grade of facial improvement was seen in 76%, 71% and 40% respectively. Lactic acid also improved mottled pigment and roughness on the forearms. Benefits were modest and the creams well tolerated.

studies.title: Effects of alpha-hydroxy acids on photoaged skin: a pilot clinical, histologic, and ultrastructural study.
studies.authors: Ditre CM, Griffin TD, Murphy GF, Sueki H, Telegan B, Johnson WC, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Lotions with 25% glycolic, lactic or citric acid applied to one forearm versus placebo on the other for about 6 months increased skin thickness by about 25%, with denser collagen and better elastic fibres on biopsy.

studies.title: Topical glycolic acid enhances photodamage by ultraviolet light.
studies.authors: Kaidbey K, Sutherland B, Bennett P, Wamer WG, Barton C, Dennis D, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In 29 adults, 4 weeks of 10% glycolic acid (pH 3.5) increased UV-induced sunburn cells and lowered the dose of UV needed to cause redness versus placebo; the effect was gone a week after stopping.

studies.title: Applications of hydroxy acids: classification, mechanisms, and photoactivity.
studies.authors: Kornhauser A, Coelho SG, Hearing VJ
studies.finding_summary: Reviews alpha-hydroxy, beta-hydroxy and polyhydroxy acids, their uses for photoaging, acne and pigmentation, and their effects on sun sensitivity, noting that their mechanisms of action still need clarification.

name: Grapefruit extract
summary: A citrus extract used for scent and a 'clarifying' image in shampoos and cleansers. No evidence of a health or hair benefit.
what: Grapefruit fruit or peel extract adds fragrance and supports marketing about 'clarifying' or 'volumising'. It is not the same as grapefruit seed extract, which is sold as a preservative.

evidence.summary: No clinical studies support hair or skin benefits of grapefruit extract at cosmetic levels. It is mainly a fragrance and marketing ingredient.

uses.note: Cleansing comes from the shampoo's surfactants.

safety: Citrus extracts contain fragrance allergens such as limonene; people with fragrance allergy may react.
Citrus peel oils can make skin more sensitive to sunlight in leave-on products; rinse-off use is not a concern.

name: Grapefruit seed extract
summary: Sold as a natural antimicrobial, but lab tests found the antimicrobial power of commercial extracts came from synthetic preservatives mixed in, not the grapefruit.
what:
Grapefruit seed extract is marketed as a natural preservative and germ-fighter in toothpastes and skin products. Independent laboratory analyses of commercial extracts repeatedly found synthetic antimicrobials (benzethonium chloride, sometimes triclosan or methylparaben) at up to about 22%.

When researchers tested an uncontaminated commercial extract, and extracts they made themselves from grapefruit seed and pulp, they found no antimicrobial activity.

evidence.summary: No clinical evidence supports an oral-health benefit. Laboratory studies indicate that genuine grapefruit seed extract has little or no antimicrobial effect and that commercial extracts' activity came from undeclared synthetic preservatives. Supply quality today may differ, but the burden of proof is on the product.

uses.use: Natural antibacterial for teeth and gums
uses.note: Antimicrobial activity traced to synthetic additives; pure extract showed none.
Can preserve a product if it contains undeclared synthetic preservatives, which defeats the 'natural' claim.

safety: Undeclared preservatives mean people allergic to them (for example quaternary ammonium compounds or parabens) cannot rule them out.
Choose toothpaste for its fluoride, not for this ingredient.

studies.title: Aspects of the antimicrobial efficacy of grapefruit seed extract and its relation to preservative substances contained.
studies.authors: von Woedtke T, Schluter B, Pflegel P, Lindequist U, Julich WD
studies.finding_summary: Five of six commercial grapefruit seed extracts killed a broad range of microbes, and every active one contained the synthetic preservative benzethonium chloride (some also triclosan and methylparaben). The one clean extract, and home-made extracts, had no antimicrobial activity.

studies.title: Simultaneous identification and quantification by liquid chromatography of benzethonium chloride, methyl paraben and triclosan in commercial products labeled as grapefruit seed extract.
studies.authors: Avula B, Dentali S, Khan IA
studies.finding_summary: Commercial products labelled grapefruit seed extract contained benzethonium chloride at 0.29-21.84%, and two contained triclosan.

name: Green tea extract
summary: Rich in the polyphenol EGCG, a strong antioxidant in the lab. Small studies hint at help for acne; anti-aging results in people have been disappointing.
what:
Green tea's catechins, especially **EGCG**, neutralize oxidants, calm inflammation and reduce sebum and acne-bacteria activity in lab studies. Extracts go into cleansers, toners, sunscreens and moisturizers, often at low, unstated levels, and catechins oxidize easily.

A concentrated green-tea catechin ointment exists as a prescription drug for genital warts; that is a far higher dose and a different product from cosmetic extracts.

evidence.summary: An 8-week trial of 10% green tea cream plus oral green tea found no visible improvement in photoaging over placebo, only changes on biopsy. A small uncontrolled study of 2% green tea lotion found fewer acne lesions after 6 weeks. Lab evidence is strong; clinical evidence at cosmetic doses is limited.

uses.note: The best-controlled trial found no visible difference from placebo after 8 weeks.
Small, mostly uncontrolled studies report fewer lesions with 2% lotions.
Reduces UV damage markers in lab and small human studies; it is not a sunscreen.
Reduces sebum in lab work; little good human data.

safety: Generally well tolerated, though the green tea group in one trial reported more irritation than placebo.

studies.title: Double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of green tea extracts in the clinical and histologic appearance of photoaging skin.
studies.authors: Chiu AE, Chan JL, Kern DG, Kohler S, Rehmus WE, Kimball AB
studies.finding_summary: 40 women with moderate photoaging used 10% green tea cream plus 300 mg oral green tea twice daily, or placebo, for 8 weeks; no clinical difference was seen, only improved elastic tissue on biopsy, and the green tea group reported more irritation.

studies.title: The efficacy of topical 2% green tea lotion in mild-to-moderate acne vulgaris.
studies.authors: Elsaie ML, Abdelhamid MF, Elsaaiee LT, Emam HM
studies.finding_summary: 20 patients with mild-to-moderate acne applied 2% green tea lotion twice daily for 6 weeks; the average lesion count fell from 24 to 10. There was no control group.

name: Homosalate
summary: A weak UVB filter used in high amounts in many US sunscreens. Well absorbed and weakly hormone-active in lab tests; the EU now limits it to 7.34% in face products only.
what:
Homosalate absorbs UVB (peak around 306 nm) and helps dissolve other filters. Because it is weak, US formulas may use a lot of it (the US allows up to 15%).

It is one of the more absorbed filters (blood levels around 14-23 ng/mL in the FDA trial) and showed weak oestrogen-like activity in cell studies. After its safety committee's review, the EU cut its maximum to 7.34% and only in face products (not body products or propellant sprays), with the change fully in force from July 2025.

evidence.summary: UVB absorption is well established, but homosalate contributes modestly to protection per percent used. Endocrine concerns come from cell and animal studies; there are no human studies showing hormonal effects from sunscreen use. The EU restriction is precautionary, based on margin-of-safety calculations. FDA lists it as needing more data.

uses.note: A supporting filter; needs partners for broad-spectrum protection.
Weak activity in cell studies only; no human evidence at sunscreen exposures.

typical: Up to 15% (US); EU maximum 7.34%, face products only
safety: If you want to limit absorbed filters (for example during pregnancy or for young children), choose mineral filters or the newer large-molecule filters. This is a precaution, not a response to proven harm.
Do not skip sun protection over absorption worries; UV damage is the proven harm.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

studies.title: In vitro and in vivo estrogenicity of UV screens.
studies.authors: Schlumpf M, Cotton B, Conscience M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Oxybenzone, homosalate, octinoxate and two other filters made breast-cancer cells proliferate in a dish; in immature rats, octinoxate and oxybenzone raised uterine weight only at very high oral doses (around 935 and 1,525 mg/kg/day). Avobenzone was inactive. Hazard screening, not evidence of effects at human exposure.

name: Hydrated silica
summary: The standard toothpaste abrasive and thickener. It scrubs off plaque and surface stain; how harsh a paste is depends on the grade, which labels rarely show.
what:
Hydrated silica is a synthetic, non-crystalline form of silica ground to fine particles. Grades differ: some mainly thicken the paste, others are cleaning abrasives. It is compatible with every type of fluoride, which is why it is the most common abrasive.

Abrasiveness is measured as RDA (relative dentin abrasivity). International standards cap toothpaste at 250; most everyday pastes sit well below that, while 'whitening' pastes are often higher. It is not the crystalline silica dust linked to lung disease, and there is no inhalation risk in a paste.

evidence.summary: Abrasives are what let toothpaste remove extrinsic stain and help brushing clear plaque, shown in lab and short clinical stain studies. Much of the literature comes from manufacturers. Whether a particular paste's abrasivity wears exposed root surfaces over years is not well studied in people.

uses.note: Its cleaning action is how most 'whitening' toothpastes work: they remove stain; they don't change tooth colour.

uses.use: Whitens teeth beyond their natural shade
uses.note: Only peroxide bleaching changes intrinsic colour.
Within the 250 RDA limit, wear on healthy enamel is small; exposed dentine and hard brushing are the real risk.

typical: Roughly 10-25% of a toothpaste (combined cleaning and thickening grades)
safety: If you have receding gums, exposed roots, erosion or sensitivity, choose a low-abrasion paste and a soft brush; ask your dentist, as RDA is rarely printed on the tube.
Brushing hard does more damage than the abrasive grade.

studies.title: Whitening toothpastes: a review of the literature.
studies.authors: Joiner A
studies.finding_summary: The abrasive system is the key functional ingredient of whitening toothpastes, designed to remove extrinsic stain without undue wear; peroxides, enzymes, pyrophosphates or optical agents may be added. Clinical tests typically run 2-6 weeks and measure surface stain.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
summary: The only ingredient that actually bleaches teeth lighter. Works in strips and trays; in toothpaste and rinses contact time is too short to do much.
what:
Hydrogen peroxide diffuses into enamel and dentine and breaks down the pigment molecules that make teeth look yellow. It changes the tooth's own colour, unlike abrasives, which only remove surface stain. Carbamide peroxide releases roughly a third of its weight as hydrogen peroxide.

Results depend on strength and contact time. Strips and trays hold gel on teeth for 30 minutes or more; a toothpaste or mouthwash is rinsed off within minutes. In the EU, products sold freely may contain at most 0.1% hydrogen peroxide; 0.1-6% is dentist-supervised only and not for under-18s.

evidence.summary: A Cochrane review found home peroxide strips and tray gels whiten teeth versus placebo, with stronger products working better. All included trials were manufacturer-sponsored, short-term and mostly at high risk of bias, and long-term harms have not been studied well. Evidence for low-level peroxide in toothpaste and rinses is thinner.

uses.note: Effective over about 2 weeks; results fade over months.
Low strength and short contact; any visible effect is small and slow.
Restorations do not bleach, so a mismatch can appear.

typical: Freely sold EU oral products at most 0.1%; US over-the-counter strips often around 6-10%, sometimes higher
safety: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are common and usually settle after stopping; a potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride paste can help.
Get a dental check before whitening: bleaching over untreated decay or gum disease can hurt and mask problems.
Not for children or teenagers (EU rules bar products above 0.1% for under-18s), or during pregnancy as a precaution.
Do not swallow whitening gels or rinses; keep them away from children.

studies.title: Home-based chemically-induced whitening of teeth in adults.
studies.authors: Hasson H, Ismail AI, Neiva G
studies.finding_summary: 25 short-term trials, all manufacturer-sponsored and mostly at high risk of bias: peroxide strips and tray gels whiten teeth versus placebo, with differences driven by peroxide strength. Mild-to-moderate tooth sensitivity and gum irritation were the common side effects.

name: Kaolin clay
summary: A soft white clay that soaks up surface oil in masks and adds body to toothpaste. It works physically; it doesn't draw out toxins or shrink pores.
what:
Kaolin is a fine, mild clay mineral. In face masks it absorbs sebum and dirt from the surface as it dries, leaving skin matte for a while; it is gentler and less drying than bentonite clay. In toothpastes and tabs it adds body and a mild polishing effect.

The effect is physical and temporary: oil returns within hours, and clay doesn't pull 'toxins' out of skin.

evidence.summary: Its oil-absorbing capacity is a known physical property, but controlled trials of kaolin masks for acne or pore appearance are essentially absent.

uses.note: A temporary matte effect from simple absorption.
Skin doesn't store toxins that clay can draw out.
Often paired with salicylic acid, which is the actual acne active.

safety: Can dry and tighten skin; limit masks to once or twice a week if your skin is dry or sensitive.

name: Keratin
summary: Protein fragments (usually from wool or feathers) that coat and fill damaged hair so it feels smoother and breaks less. A cosmetic effect that washes out.
what:
Hair is itself made of keratin. Products add keratin broken into smaller pieces ('hydrolysed'), which stick to the hair surface and, if small enough, slip a little way into damaged cuticle. Hair feels smoother, looks shinier and may break less while the coating lasts.

This is different from salon 'keratin smoothing' or 'Brazilian' treatments, whose straightening effect usually comes from formaldehyde-releasing chemicals heated into the hair, not from keratin.

evidence.summary: Laboratory tests, mostly by ingredient makers, show hydrolysed keratin binds to hair and improves strength, gloss and combing. There are no independent trials on long-term hair health, and nothing shows it rebuilds hair structure or affects growth.

uses.note: A real but temporary conditioning effect.
It fills and coats damaged areas for a while; hair cannot actually repair itself.
It acts on the hair shaft, not the follicle.

typical: Usually under 1-2% in shampoos, conditioners and treatments
safety: Keratin in shampoo and conditioner is very low risk.

Salon keratin smoothing treatments are a different product: the FDA has warned that many release formaldehyde when heated, causing eye, nose and throat irritation. Ask what is in them, and consider avoiding them during pregnancy.
Heavy protein products can make fine hair feel stiff; alternate with a moisturising conditioner.

name: Lactic acid (ammonium lactate)
summary: A gentler AHA that also draws in water. As a 12% ammonium lactate lotion it has good trial evidence for very dry, rough and scaly skin.
what:
Lactic acid is an AHA slightly larger than glycolic acid and part of the skin's own natural moisturizing factor, so besides loosening dead cells it acts as a humectant. **Ammonium lactate** is lactic acid partly neutralized with ammonia; at 12% it is a long-standing treatment for severe dry skin (xerosis), rough bumpy skin on the arms and legs, and inherited scaling conditions.

It shows up mostly in body lotions and 'smoothing' creams for rough skin.

evidence.summary: A double-blind trial found 12% ammonium lactate lotion outperformed 5% lactic acid lotion for moderate to severe dry skin, with benefits lasting through a 3-week break. An 8% L-lactic acid cream modestly improved photodamage, mottled pigment and roughness in a 22-week vehicle-controlled trial. The trials are older and moderate in size.

uses.use: Very dry, rough or scaly skin
uses.note: 12% ammonium lactate beat 5% lactic acid for moderate to severe dryness over 3 weeks.
Commonly recommended and softens the bumps; they usually return when you stop.
8% L-lactic acid cream beat vehicle on photodamage and mottled pigment over 22 weeks.

works_with: A thick moisturizer on very dry skin
safety: Stings on cracked, freshly shaved or broken skin; apply to intact skin.
Like other AHAs it can increase sun sensitivity; use sunscreen on exposed areas.
Avoid on inflamed eczema.

studies.title: Comparative efficacy of 12% ammonium lactate lotion and 5% lactic acid lotion in the treatment of moderate to severe xerosis.
studies.authors: Rogers RS 3rd, Callen J, Wehr R, Krochmal L
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: In a double-blind trial in moderate to severe dry skin, 12% ammonium lactate lotion twice daily reduced xerosis more than 5% lactic acid lotion over 3 weeks, and the advantage held through a 3-week no-treatment period.

studies.title: Topical 8% glycolic acid and 8% L-lactic acid creams for the treatment of photodamaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled clinical trial.
studies.authors: Stiller MJ, Bartolone J, Stern R, Smith S, Kollias N, Gillies R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 74 women with photodamaged skin used 8% glycolic acid, 8% L-lactic acid or vehicle cream twice daily for 22 weeks; at least one grade of facial improvement was seen in 76%, 71% and 40% respectively. Lactic acid also improved mottled pigment and roughness on the forearms. Benefits were modest and the creams well tolerated.

name: Lavender oil
summary: Mostly a fragrance. There's no good evidence it treats skin, and air-oxidized lavender oil forms strong contact allergens.
what:
Lavender essential oil is mainly linalool and linalyl acetate. In body washes, lotions, soaps and deodorants it is there for scent, sometimes with 'calming' or 'bedtime' positioning.
