Those terpenes react with air to form hydroperoxides, which are potent skin sensitizers, so older, air-exposed oil is more likely to cause allergy than fresh oil. Lavender products have also been linked in case reports to breast growth in children who used them regularly.

evidence.summary: There are no good trials showing lavender oil improves any skin condition when used in personal-care products, and aromatherapy findings don't transfer to a short wash-off exposure. Its allergy risk after oxidation is well documented. Case reports link regular lavender-product use with reversible breast growth in children, but causation is unproven.

uses.note: No good trials in personal-care products.

uses.use: Relaxation or better sleep from scented products
uses.note: Aromatherapy research is mixed, and the brief exposure from a wash or lotion hasn't been tested.
Lab activity only; not shown to matter in products.

safety: Oxidized lavender oil is a significant contact allergen; people with fragrance allergy, especially to linalool, should avoid it.

Case reports describe breast growth in prepubertal boys and girls using lavender products regularly, resolving after stopping. The link is not proven, but limiting use in young children is a cautious choice.
Essential oils count as fragrance, even in products marketed as 'natural'.

studies.title: Lavender oil lacks natural protection against autoxidation, forming strong contact allergens on air exposure.
studies.authors: Hagvall L, Sköld M, Bråred-Christensson J, Börje A, Karlberg AT
studies.finding_summary: Lavender oil's terpenes oxidized on air exposure to form hydroperoxides, raising its sensitizing potency in mice; patients allergic to oxidized linalool reacted on patch testing to air-exposed lavender oil.

studies.title: Prepubertal gynecomastia linked to lavender and tea tree oils.
studies.authors: Henley DV, Lipson N, Korach KS, Bloch CA
studies.finding_summary: Three prepubertal boys developed breast enlargement while using products containing lavender and tea tree oils; it resolved after they stopped, and both oils showed weak estrogenic and anti-androgenic activity in human cell lines. Causation was disputed in later correspondence.

studies.title: Lavender Products Associated With Premature Thelarche and Prepubertal Gynecomastia: Case Reports and Endocrine-Disrupting Chemical Activities.
studies.authors: Ramsey JT, Li Y, Arao Y, Naidu A, Coons LA, Diaz A, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
studies.finding_summary: Three girls and one boy with early breast growth and continuous exposure to lavender-fragranced products improved after stopping; several essential-oil components had estrogenic or anti-androgenic effects in cell lines, but whether real-world exposure is enough is unknown.

name: Lemon peel oil
summary: A citrus flavouring in toothpaste and mouthwash. Adds taste; no oral-health effect has been shown.
what: Lemon peel oil is pressed from lemon rind and used for flavour and scent. Its main components (limonene and citral) are common fragrance allergens, which is why EU labels must name them above set levels.

evidence.summary: There is no clinical evidence that lemon oil in oral-care products benefits teeth or gums. It is a flavouring.

uses.note: That is its job.
No evidence; acidic lemon juice (not the oil) can erode enamel.

safety: People allergic to fragrance components (limonene, citral) may react with lip or mouth irritation.
Cold-pressed lemon oil makes skin sensitive to sunlight in leave-on skin products; this is not a concern in toothpaste that is rinsed away.

name: Licorice root extract
summary: A soothing, mildly brightening plant extract. Its compounds calm redness and slow pigment in the lab; human evidence at cosmetic doses is small.
what:
Licorice root extract contains **glabridin**, which inhibits tyrosinase and calms inflammation, and **liquiritin**, which disperses melanin. It is used in brightening and anti-redness products, usually at low levels among other actives, and extract strength varies widely between suppliers.

Licochalcone A, behind many anti-redness claims, comes mainly from a related licorice species; it is not what 'Glycyrrhiza glabra root extract' on a label reliably contains.

evidence.summary: Lab studies support anti-pigment and anti-inflammatory activity. Human data are a few small studies, mostly of concentrated purified licorice compounds rather than the low-dose extracts in most products.

uses.note: Good lab evidence; thin human evidence at cosmetic doses.
Anti-inflammatory in lab studies; not well tested alone in people.

safety: Eating large amounts of licorice can raise blood pressure; that is not a known risk from skin products.
Plant extracts can cause contact allergy; patch test if your skin is reactive.

name: Mandelic acid
summary: A larger, slower-penetrating AHA often chosen for sensitive or darker skin. Used in acne peels and now in deodorants that lower skin pH.
what:
Mandelic acid is an AHA with a bulky ring structure, so it penetrates more slowly than glycolic acid and tends to sting less. It also has some antibacterial activity. Clinics use it in peels, often combined with salicylic acid, for acne and pigmentation, especially in darker skin where irritation-driven darkening is a concern.

In body care it appears mainly in 'whole-body' deodorants and washes, where the acid is meant to lower skin pH and slow the bacteria that cause odour rather than to exfoliate.

evidence.summary: Evidence comes mostly from small peel studies. In a 44-patient comparison, a 20% salicylic–10% mandelic acid peel beat a 35% glycolic peel for active acne and post-acne dark marks with fewer side effects; a Cochrane review, looking at participant-rated improvement, found little difference and rated the evidence low quality. Leave-on mandelic products and mandelic deodorants have little published testing.

uses.note: Salicylic-mandelic peels helped acne in a small comparative trial; the combination makes it hard to credit mandelic acid alone.
Improved in the same small peel trial.
Its slower penetration makes it milder in practice, but head-to-head tolerability trials are few.
Lowering skin pH plausibly slows odour bacteria, but independent trials of mandelic acid deodorants are lacking.

safety: Like other AHAs it can increase sun sensitivity; use sunscreen on exposed skin.
Underarm use can sting right after shaving; apply to unbroken skin.

studies.title: Glycolic acid peels versus salicylic-mandelic acid peels in active acne vulgaris and post-acne scarring and hyperpigmentation: a comparative study.
studies.authors: Garg VK, Sinha S, Sarkar R
studies.finding_summary: 44 patients in India with acne and post-acne marks had six fortnightly peels of 35% glycolic acid or 20% salicylic–10% mandelic acid; both helped, and the salicylic-mandelic peel worked better on active acne and pigmentation with fewer side effects.

studies.title: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne.
studies.authors: Liu H, Yu H, Xia J, Liu L, Liu GJ, Sang H, Peinemann F
studies.finding_summary: 49 trials (3,880 people): azelaic acid is probably less effective than benzoyl peroxide and about as effective as tretinoin for acne; evidence for salicylic acid, nicotinamide and alpha-hydroxy acids was low or very low quality, from small head-to-head trials, and no conclusions were reported for zinc or sulphur.

name: Niacinamide
summary: A form of vitamin B3 that, at 2-5%, modestly evens blotchy tone, cuts oiliness and supports the skin barrier. Well tolerated by most skin.
what:
Niacinamide is the amide form of vitamin B3. In skin it feeds the NAD cofactors cells use for energy and repair, and it nudges the outer layer to make more **ceramides** and other barrier lipids. It is water-soluble, stable in most formulas and rarely irritating, which is why it turns up in everything from toners to body lotions.

It is not an exfoliant or a retinoid, so it works slowly: most trials run 4-12 weeks and measure small, real changes — fewer blotches, a less oily T-zone, better-hydrated skin. Serums at 10% or more are common, but the controlled studies used 2-5%, and higher strengths mainly raise the odds of stinging and redness.

evidence.summary: Several randomized, vehicle-controlled split-face trials (roughly 20-100 people, 4-12 weeks) found 2-5% niacinamide reduced hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness, sebum and fine lines. Most were run or funded by one large skincare maker, the effects are modest, and few trials compare it with established drugs. A 2020 Cochrane review rated the acne evidence low quality.

uses.note: 5% reduced hyperpigmentation versus vehicle within 4-8 weeks in controlled trials. It blocks pigment transfer to skin cells rather than melanin production, so results are gradual and modest.
Raises ceramide production and reduced red blotchiness in trials; a sensible choice for dry or easily irritated skin.
2% lowered sebum output in a Japanese trial; in a US trial it reduced surface oil but not sebum output.
A 4% gel did about as well as a clindamycin gel in an older trial, but a Cochrane review rated the acne evidence low quality. Use it alongside proven acne treatments, not instead of them.
One 12-week split-face trial at 5% found small improvements; the evidence is far weaker than for retinoids.
Pores can look smaller when skin is less oily, but pore size itself has not been a well-measured trial outcome.

works_with: Retinoids — may make them easier to tolerate
Sunscreen — essential in any dark-spot routine
Vitamin C — the old warning that the two cancel out came from high-temperature lab chemistry, not skin
safety: Serums at 10% and above cause stinging, redness or breakouts in some people; switch to a 2-5% product if that happens.
No specific pregnancy concerns are known for topical use.

studies.title: Niacinamide: A B vitamin that improves aging facial skin appearance.
studies.authors: Bissett DL, Oblong JE, Berge CA
studies.finding_summary: 50 women with photoaged skin applied 5% niacinamide to one side of the face and vehicle to the other for 12 weeks; niacinamide reduced fine lines, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness and sallowness and improved elasticity. Run by a skincare manufacturer.

studies.title: The effect of niacinamide on reducing cutaneous pigmentation and suppression of melanosome transfer.
studies.authors: Hakozaki T, Minwalla L, Zhuang J, Chhoa M, Matsubara A, Miyamoto K, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Niacinamide did not block melanin production but inhibited pigment transfer to skin cells by 35-68% in a lab model; in 18 people using 5% and 120 people using 2% with sunscreen, it reduced facial hyperpigmentation versus vehicle within 4 weeks.

studies.title: The effect of 2% niacinamide on facial sebum production.
studies.authors: Draelos ZD, Matsubara A, Smiles K
studies.journal: Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy
studies.finding_summary: In 100 Japanese adults, a 2% niacinamide moisturizer lowered sebum excretion rate versus placebo over 4 weeks; in a 6-week split-face study of 30 white adults it reduced surface oil but not sebum excretion rate.

studies.title: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne.
studies.authors: Liu H, Yu H, Xia J, Liu L, Liu GJ, Sang H, Peinemann F
studies.finding_summary: 49 trials (3,880 people): azelaic acid is probably less effective than benzoyl peroxide and about as effective as tretinoin for acne; evidence for salicylic acid, nicotinamide and alpha-hydroxy acids was low or very low quality, from small head-to-head trials, and no conclusions were reported for zinc or sulphur.

name: Octinoxate
summary: A long-used UVB filter, and part of the sunscreen that cut skin cancer in the landmark trial. Unstable next to avobenzone; banned in Hawaii over reef concerns.
what:
Octinoxate is a cinnamate that absorbs UVB (peak around 310 nm). It has been one of the most widely used filters worldwide and is also added in small amounts to perfumes (where this catalogue lists it) and hair products to protect the product from light.

It degrades in sunlight, and it destabilises avobenzone when the two are combined without a stabiliser. Hawaii banned sunscreens containing it (and oxybenzone) from 2021 over coral-reef concerns.

evidence.summary: The Nambour randomised trial sunscreen was 8% octinoxate + 2% avobenzone, and it reduced squamous-cell cancer and photoageing. Octinoxate is absorbed (around 5-8 ng/mL in the FDA trial) and is oestrogen-active in lab and high-dose rodent studies, but a human whole-body study at 10% found no hormone changes, and the EU's safety committee in 2025 concluded it is safe up to 10% given the large margin of safety. FDA lists it as needing more data.

uses.note: Effective, but loses strength with sun exposure.
Seen in cells and in rats at very high oral doses; a human study at 10% whole-body use found no attributable hormone change.
Mainly lab evidence at concentrations above most measured reef levels; bans are precautionary.

avoid_with: avobenzone, unless the formula includes a stabiliser such as octocrylene or bemotrizinol
safety: Allergy is uncommon.
Sunscreens with it cannot be sold in Hawaii (and some other jurisdictions); check local rules when travelling.
Those limiting absorbed filters can choose mineral or newer large-molecule filters as a precaution.

studies.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial.
studies.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, Green AC
studies.finding_summary: In 903 adults under 55, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years led to 24% less skin ageing (measured by skin-surface microtopography) than discretionary use; the daily group showed no detectable increase in ageing over the trial.

studies.title: Systemic absorption of the sunscreens benzophenone-3, octyl-methoxycinnamate, and 3-(4-methyl-benzylidene) camphor after whole-body topical application and reproductive hormone levels in humans.
studies.authors: Janjua NR, Mogensen B, Andersson AM, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 32 volunteers applied cream with 10% each of oxybenzone, octinoxate and 4-MBC over the whole body daily for a week. All three were absorbed (oxybenzone up to 200-300 ng/mL), but reproductive hormones showed no changes attributable to the filters.

studies.title: In vitro and in vivo estrogenicity of UV screens.
studies.authors: Schlumpf M, Cotton B, Conscience M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Oxybenzone, homosalate, octinoxate and two other filters made breast-cancer cells proliferate in a dish; in immature rats, octinoxate and oxybenzone raised uterine weight only at very high oral doses (around 935 and 1,525 mg/kg/day). Avobenzone was inactive. Hazard screening, not evidence of effects at human exposure.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

name: Octisalate
summary: A weak UVB filter used mainly to top up SPF and help dissolve other filters. Low allergy risk; absorbed, like most organic filters.
what:
Octisalate is a salicylate that absorbs UVB (peak around 307 nm). It is weak on its own, so it is almost always one of several filters, adding a little SPF and acting as a solvent that keeps crystalline filters such as avobenzone dissolved.

In perfumes it is added in small amounts to protect the scent and colour from light.

evidence.summary: Its UVB absorption is well characterised, but its contribution to a product's protection is modest. The FDA trial found blood levels around 5 ng/mL, above the screening threshold. There is no human evidence of harm; FDA lists it as needing more safety data.

uses.note: A supporting filter; the product's SPF depends on the whole combination.
It barely absorbs UVA; broad-spectrum claims rely on other filters.

safety: Allergy is rare.
No special restrictions for children beyond general sunscreen advice (shade first under 6 months).

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

name: Octocrylene
summary: UVB filter mostly used to stabilise avobenzone. Effective, but can break down to benzophenone in the bottle and occasionally causes photoallergy.
what:
Octocrylene absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA2 and, just as important, it stabilises avobenzone so the UVA protection lasts in sunlight. It also helps dissolve other filters.

Two things put it under scrutiny. Lab work found that it slowly degrades to **benzophenone** (a suspected carcinogen) in the bottle, rising as products age. And it is a known, if uncommon, cause of photoallergic rashes.

evidence.summary: Its UV absorption and stabilising role are well established in formulation testing and SPF measurement. It is absorbed into the blood (around 7 ng/mL in the FDA trial), above the screening threshold. Benzophenone formation comes from one lab group's analysis of products and has been disputed in published letters; no study has measured health effects in users. FDA lists it as needing more data; the EU caps it at 10% (9% in propellant sprays) and requires benzophenone to be kept at trace level.

uses.note: Its main value is keeping avobenzone working through sun exposure.
Shown in one lab study of 16 products (amount rose with ageing); disputed, and not linked to harm in users. Using sunscreen within its shelf life and not storing it hot limits degradation.
Some aquatic studies show effects at high concentrations; field-relevant risk is not established.

typical: Up to 10% (US and EU; EU 9% in propellant sprays)
safety: Photoallergy is the main risk, especially if you have ever reacted to ketoprofen gel (a topical anti-inflammatory): choose an octocrylene-free product.
Children occasionally develop contact allergy from octocrylene sunscreens; if a rash appears where sunscreen was applied, see a clinician for patch testing.
Discard sunscreen past its expiry date or after it has been stored hot.

studies.title: Benzophenone Accumulates over Time from the Degradation of Octocrylene in Commercial Sunscreen Products.
studies.authors: Downs CA, DiNardo JC, Stien D, Rodrigues AMS, Lebaron P
studies.finding_summary: Sixteen octocrylene-containing sunscreens from the EU and US contained benzophenone at an average 39 mg/kg, rising to 75 mg/kg after an accelerated-ageing protocol; a product without octocrylene had none. Shows a degradation pathway in the bottle, not a measured harm to users; the paper drew published critical letters.

studies.title: Contact and photocontact allergy to octocrylene: a review.
studies.authors: de Groot AC, Roberts DW
studies.finding_summary: Photocontact allergy to octocrylene has been reported increasingly since 2003, mainly in adults previously sensitised to the anti-inflammatory gel ketoprofen; plain contact allergy is rarer and seen mostly in children using octocrylene sunscreens.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

name: Other fruit acids (tartaric, malic)
summary: Grape and apple acids, usually minor parts of acid blends. Weaker exfoliants than glycolic or lactic acid, with little evidence on their own.
what:
Tartaric acid (from grapes) and malic acid (from apples) are alpha-hydroxy acids that turn up in multi-acid blends and 'fruit extract' complexes. They are larger and weaker than glycolic and lactic acid, and in many formulas they mainly adjust pH rather than exfoliate much.

When a label says just **AHA**, it rarely states which acids or how much; judge the product by its full ingredient list and stated pH, if any.

evidence.summary: Nearly all clinical AHA evidence is for glycolic and lactic acid. Tartaric and malic acid have lab data and appear in combination products, but trials testing them alone are scarce, so their contribution to a blend is uncertain.

uses.note: They add some acid activity, but blends are rarely tested ingredient by ingredient.
No good trials of these acids alone.

safety: Like all AHAs they can sting and increase sun sensitivity; use sunscreen.
Layering several acid products raises irritation without clear extra benefit.

studies.title: Applications of hydroxy acids: classification, mechanisms, and photoactivity.
studies.authors: Kornhauser A, Coelho SG, Hearing VJ
studies.finding_summary: Reviews alpha-hydroxy, beta-hydroxy and polyhydroxy acids, their uses for photoaging, acne and pigmentation, and their effects on sun sensitivity, noting that their mechanisms of action still need clarification.

name: Oxybenzone
summary: The most absorbed and most debated sunscreen filter: effective, but a known photoallergen, restricted in the EU and banned in Hawaii. Evidence of human harm is lacking.
what:
Oxybenzone absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA2. It has fallen out of favour: it reaches far higher blood levels than any other filter (around 258 ng/mL from lotion in the FDA trial, some 500 times the screening threshold), it was detectable in the urine of 97% of Americans tested in 2003-04, and it is a well-known cause of allergic and photoallergic rashes.

The EU limits it to 6% in face, hand and lip products and 2.2% in body products. Hawaii and the US Virgin Islands banned sunscreens containing it over reef concerns.

evidence.summary: It is an effective UVB/UVA2 filter. Hormone concerns come from cell studies and rats fed very high doses; a human study with 10% whole-body application found no attributable hormone change. Reef harm rests mainly on lab studies of coral larvae, often at concentrations above those measured on most reefs; a critical 2021 review called the risk evidence incomplete. High absorption is well documented, harm at real exposures is not, and plenty of alternatives exist.

uses.note: Effective, but covers little long-wave UVA1 without partners.
Weak effects in cells and high-dose rat studies; not shown in the one human trial that measured hormones.
Toxic to coral larvae in the lab; how much it contributes to reef decline next to warming and pollution is unknown.
A recognised contact and photocontact allergen; about 0.5% of patients patch-tested for dermatitis react to it.

typical: Up to 6% (US); EU 6% face/hand/lip, 2.2% body products
safety: Avoid it if you have had a rash from a sunscreen or are prone to allergic skin; ask a clinician about patch testing.
If you prefer to minimise absorbed filters (pregnancy, young children), oxybenzone is the one to avoid first. That is a precaution; harm is not proven.
Sunscreens containing it cannot be sold in Hawaii or the US Virgin Islands.

studies.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 48 healthy adults applied one of four sunscreens to 75% of the body, up to 4 times a day for 4 days. Avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate all exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after a single application; oxybenzone reached about 258 ng/mL from lotion. The authors state this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

studies.title: Systemic absorption of the sunscreens benzophenone-3, octyl-methoxycinnamate, and 3-(4-methyl-benzylidene) camphor after whole-body topical application and reproductive hormone levels in humans.
studies.authors: Janjua NR, Mogensen B, Andersson AM, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 32 volunteers applied cream with 10% each of oxybenzone, octinoxate and 4-MBC over the whole body daily for a week. All three were absorbed (oxybenzone up to 200-300 ng/mL), but reproductive hormones showed no changes attributable to the filters.

studies.title: Toxicopathological Effects of the Sunscreen UV Filter, Oxybenzone (Benzophenone-3), on Coral Planulae and Cultured Primary Cells and Its Environmental Contamination in Hawaii and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
studies.authors: Downs CA, Kramarsky-Winter E, Segal R, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In the lab, oxybenzone deformed and bleached coral larvae, with effects worse in light; some effect levels were in the low micrograms per litre. Water at some Virgin Islands sites measured far higher than Hawaiian sites. This is the study behind many reef bans.

studies.title: A Critical Review of Organic Ultraviolet Filter Exposure, Hazard, and Risk to Corals.
studies.authors: Mitchelmore CL, Burns EE, Conway A, Heyes A, Davies IA
studies.finding_summary: Across 12 studies, UV filters near reefs were mostly found in the nanograms-per-litre range, while toxic effects in the nine coral toxicity papers appeared at micrograms to milligrams per litre, with widely varying methods. The authors list major data gaps and flawed assumptions and call for better studies before firm risk conclusions.

name: Panthenol (provitamin B5)
summary: Provitamin B5: a humectant that helps skin hold water and recover from irritation. Very well tolerated, with small but consistent studies.
what:
Panthenol is converted in skin to pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), part of coenzyme A, which cells use to make barrier lipids. It is also a humectant in its own right, penetrates skin well and very rarely irritates. **Dexpanthenol** is its active form; 'vitamin B5' on a lotion label usually means panthenol.

You'll find it in body lotions, lip and nappy balms, after-sun and hair products, typically at 0.5-5%.

evidence.summary: Small controlled studies show dexpanthenol creams speed barrier recovery after irritation, increase hydration and reduce redness compared with the same cream without it. Reviews also report benefits for minor wounds and irritated skin, though much of the research is linked to makers of dexpanthenol products.

uses.note: Improves stratum corneum hydration and reduces water loss.
Sped barrier repair and reduced redness versus vehicle after detergent irritation.
Supportive studies, mostly small.

safety: Contact allergy is rare; stop if a rash appears.

studies.title: Topical use of dexpanthenol in skin disorders.
studies.authors: Ebner F, Heller A, Rippke F, Tausch I
studies.finding_summary: Reviews topical dexpanthenol: it improves stratum corneum hydration, reduces water loss, speeds epidermal regeneration in wounds and eases irritation symptoms, with minimal risk of irritation or sensitization.

studies.title: Dexpanthenol enhances skin barrier repair and reduces inflammation after sodium lauryl sulphate-induced irritation.
studies.authors: Proksch E, Nissen HP
studies.finding_summary: After detergent (SLS) irritation, a dexpanthenol cream sped barrier repair and increased hydration more than its vehicle, and reduced redness, which the vehicle did not.

name: Peppermint oil and menthol
summary: Mint gives toothpaste its taste and shampoos their tingle via cooling receptors. It freshens; hair-growth claims rest on one mouse study.
what:
Peppermint oil is steam-distilled from the peppermint plant; menthol is its main cooling component. Both trigger the skin's cold receptors (TRPM8), producing the fresh, tingling feeling in toothpaste, mouthwash and 'invigorating' shampoos. The tingle is a sensation, not a sign that anything is being cleaned or stimulated.

At higher strengths menthol is a regulated counter-irritant in pain-relief rubs; in oral and hair care it is used at low levels.

evidence.summary: Mint's role in oral care is flavour and a feeling of freshness, which is not the same as reducing bad-breath bacteria. The widely shared claim that peppermint oil grows hair comes from a single 2014 study in mice; there are no controlled human trials.

uses.note: Masks odour briefly; it does not treat the cause of bad breath.
One mouse study; no human trials.

uses.use: Cooling, soothing scalp or skin feel
uses.note: A real sensory effect via cold receptors.

typical: Well under 1-2% in toothpaste and shampoo; 1.25-16% menthol only in pain-relief rubs
safety: Never apply peppermint oil or menthol products to the face or chest of babies and young children: they have triggered breathing problems.
Mint flavouring can cause contact allergy (sore lips, mouth ulcers or rash) in a few people; a mint-free paste settles it.
Undiluted essential oil irritates the scalp and eyes; use it only as formulated.

studies.title: Peppermint Oil Promotes Hair Growth without Toxic Signs.
studies.authors: Oh JY, Park MA, Kim YC
studies.finding_summary: In shaved mice, 3% peppermint oil applied for 4 weeks produced more hair growth, deeper and more numerous follicles than saline, jojoba oil or 3% minoxidil. No human data.

name: Peptides (signal and wrinkle-relaxing)
summary: Short amino-acid chains meant to signal skin to make collagen or to relax expression lines. Small, mostly manufacturer-run trials; effects are modest.
what:
Cosmetic peptides are short protein fragments, often with a fatty acid (palmitoyl) attached to help them into skin. **Signal peptides** (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, palmitoyl tripeptide-1, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7) mimic collagen fragments and prompt fibroblasts to make more matrix in lab tests. **Neurotransmitter-inhibiting peptides** (acetyl hexapeptide-8, pentapeptide-18) interfere with the nerve signal that contracts facial muscles — in a lab dish — and are sold as a topical alternative to wrinkle-relaxing injections. **Copper tripeptide-1** carries copper and is linked to wound healing.

Most are near or above the roughly 500-dalton size that passes easily through skin, which limits how much reaches its target, and they are used at tiny concentrations.

evidence.summary: Controlled trials are few, small and usually run by ingredient or product makers: a 12-week split-face trial in 93 women found 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 reduced fine lines versus the same moisturizer without it. Trials of the wrinkle-relaxing peptides are small, and none shows effects comparable to injections. Independent replication is scarce.

uses.note: Small improvements in a few controlled, mostly industry-run trials.
A few small trials report shallower wrinkles, but nothing shows these peptides relax muscles the way injections do, and they penetrate skin poorly.
Shown in lab tests; evidence in people is indirect.
Mostly lab and wound-healing research.

works_with: Retinoids, vitamin C and sunscreen — peptides are an add-on, not a replacement
avoid_with: Copper peptides and L-ascorbic acid in the same step — copper speeds vitamin C breakdown
safety: Generally well tolerated.
Price and the number of peptides in a product aren't a guide to its effect.

studies.title: Topical palmitoyl pentapeptide provides improvement in photoaged human facial skin.
studies.authors: Robinson LR, Fitzgerald NC, Doughty DG, Dawes NC, Berge CA, Bissett DL
studies.finding_summary: 93 women aged 35-55 used a moisturizer with 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide on one side of the face and the same moisturizer without it on the other for 12 weeks; the peptide side showed significantly fewer wrinkles and fine lines. Run by a skincare manufacturer.

studies.title: Role of topical peptides in preventing or treating aged skin.
studies.authors: Gorouhi F, Maibach HI
studies.finding_summary: Reviews controlled ex vivo and in vivo studies of topical peptides and proteins for skin aging, grouping them as signal, enzyme-inhibitor, neurotransmitter-inhibitor and carrier peptides.

studies.title: The 500 Dalton rule for the skin penetration of chemical compounds and drugs.
studies.authors: Bos JD, Meinardi MM
studies.finding_summary: Argues that a compound must weigh under about 500 daltons to pass through the skin's outer layer, based on the size of known contact allergens and of the drugs that work topically or through transdermal patches.

name: Phytosphingosine
summary: A skin-identical lipid from the ceramide family, antimicrobial and calming in lab tests. Usually a supporting ingredient in barrier creams.
what:
Phytosphingosine is a sphingoid base — one of the building blocks of ceramides, the lipids that seal the skin barrier — and occurs naturally in the skin's outer layer. It is added to barrier-repair moisturizers, often alongside ceramides and cholesterol, and to acne and scalp products.

In lab studies it inhibits acne bacteria and inflammation. Whether it adds much beyond the ceramides and occlusives it's formulated with is uncertain.

evidence.summary: The main clinical data come from a small study co-authored by the ingredient's manufacturer, reporting antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects and improvement in acne-prone skin. Independent controlled trials are lacking.

uses.note: Plausible as a ceramide building block; not tested alone.
Positive results in a small manufacturer-linked study.

safety: Well tolerated; no notable safety concerns at cosmetic levels.

studies.title: Anti-microbial and -inflammatory activity and efficacy of phytosphingosine: an in vitro and in vivo study addressing acne vulgaris.
studies.authors: Pavicic T, Wollenweber U, Farwick M, Korting HC
studies.finding_summary: Lab and small human studies, co-authored by the ingredient's manufacturer, found phytosphingosine antimicrobial against acne bacteria and anti-inflammatory, with improvements in acne-prone skin.

name: Piroctone olamine
summary: An antifungal that replaced zinc pyrithione in many European dandruff shampoos. Matched it in a manufacturer-run trial; not an approved US dandruff drug.
what:
Piroctone olamine is an antifungal that targets the Malassezia yeast behind dandruff. It is permitted in EU cosmetics (up to 1% in rinse-off products and 0.5% in others) and became the main European anti-dandruff active after zinc pyrithione was banned in 2022.

It is not among the FDA's approved dandruff actives, so US products cannot make a dandruff-treatment drug claim based on it alone; it appears in US products as a cosmetic ingredient or alongside an approved active.

evidence.summary: A split-head trial found a shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine plus 0.45% climbazole reduced dandruff as well as 1% zinc pyrithione; it was run by a manufacturer and tested a combination. Lab data show solid antifungal activity. Independent trials are few.

uses.note: Comparable to zinc pyrithione in manufacturer-run trials.
Not established.

typical: 0.5-1% in rinse-off shampoos (EU maximum 1% rinse-off, 0.5% leave-on)
safety: Generally well tolerated; keep out of the eyes.
If flaking persists or the scalp is red and inflamed, see a clinician about seborrhoeic dermatitis or psoriasis.

studies.title: Efficacy of a piroctone olamine/climbazol shampoo in comparison with a zinc pyrithione shampoo in subjects with moderate to severe dandruff.
studies.authors: Schmidt-Rose T, Braren S, Folster H, et al.
studies.finding_summary: A shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine plus 0.45% climbazole reduced dandruff as well as a 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo in a split-head study, with similar antifungal activity in the lab. Conducted by the manufacturer's research team.

name: Potassium nitrate
summary: The classic 'sensitive teeth' ingredient. It calms the tooth nerve over a few weeks of twice-daily use; the benefit is real but moderate.
what:
Tooth sensitivity happens when exposed dentine lets cold, air or touch reach the nerve through tiny tubules. Potassium ions diffuse along those tubules and damp down nerve firing. It does not block the tubules, so relief builds gradually and fades if you stop.

Most desensitising toothpastes use 5% potassium nitrate, usually alongside fluoride.

evidence.summary: An older Cochrane review of six small trials found reductions in measured sensitivity but not in patients' own ratings and called the evidence unclear. Larger network meta-analyses since (125 and 32 trials) found potassium pastes beneficial with moderate certainty, especially for touch-triggered pain, with stannous fluoride and some other agents at least as effective.

uses.note: Moderate benefit after 2-8 weeks of twice-daily brushing.
It acts on the nerve; it does not rebuild tooth structure.

safety: If sensitivity is limited to one tooth, is sharp and lingering, or does not ease within about 4 weeks, see a dentist: it can mean decay, a crack or a failing filling.
Sensitive-teeth toothpastes are not intended for young children unless a dentist advises it.

studies.title: Potassium containing toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity.
studies.authors: Poulsen S, Errboe M, Lescay Mevil Y, Glenny AM
studies.finding_summary: Six small trials: potassium nitrate paste reduced sensitivity to air blast and touch at 6-8 weeks, but patients' own ratings did not improve significantly; the authors judged the evidence insufficient for clear support.

studies.title: Desensitizing Toothpastes for Dentin Hypersensitivity: A Network Meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Martins CC, Firmino RT, Riva JJ, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 125 RCTs (12,541 patients). Compared with ordinary fluoride paste, stannous fluoride, potassium salts (alone or combined with stannous fluoride), calcium sodium phosphosilicate, arginine and strontium reduced sensitivity to at least one stimulus, with moderate-to-high certainty.

studies.title: Comparative efficacy of self-administered dentifrices for the management of dentine hypersensitivity - A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Pollard AJ, Khan I, Davies M, Claydon N, West NX
studies.finding_summary: 32 trials (4,638 adults) with standardised methods: twice-daily toothpastes containing stannous fluoride, potassium with or without stannous, or arginine can be recommended to reduce sensitivity pain.

name: Propolis
summary: A resin bees collect from plants, used for blemishes and 'glow'. Antimicrobial in the lab, little tested on skin, and a well-documented contact allergen.
what:
Propolis is the sticky resin bees gather from tree buds to seal their hives. It is rich in flavonoids and caffeic acid esters, with antibacterial, antifungal and antioxidant activity in lab tests. Korean skincare uses propolis extracts in serums and toners for blemish-prone and dull skin.

Its composition varies with region and plant source, so two 'propolis extracts' can differ considerably.

evidence.summary: Clinical evidence for propolis in cosmetic skincare is sparse — mostly lab work and small studies in wound care. Its allergy potential, by contrast, is well documented, with many reported cases of allergic contact dermatitis.

uses.note: Antibacterial in lab tests; no good trials of propolis skincare.
Marketing language without supporting trials.

safety: A known contact allergen; avoid it if you have reacted to propolis, beeswax, balsam of Peru or fragrance before.
Patch test first if you have sensitive skin or bee-product allergies.

studies.title: Propolis: a review of properties, applications, chemical composition, contact allergy, and other adverse effects.
studies.authors: de Groot AC
studies.finding_summary: Reviews propolis's composition, biological properties and uses, and catalogues its contact allergy: sensitizing potential, products causing reactions, frequency, cross-reactions and the specific allergens involved.

name: Quinoa protein
summary: A plant protein used like keratin or silk: it coats hair to make it feel stronger and smoother. Cosmetic, temporary, plant-based.
what: Hydrolysed quinoa protein is broken into small peptides that bind to the hair surface, marketed as a plant-based alternative to animal proteins. Its effect is the same kind of temporary conditioning: less frizz, easier combing, a feeling of stronger strands.

evidence.summary: Only ingredient-maker lab testing supports the conditioning claims. No evidence it affects hair growth or health.

uses.note: Typical protein-conditioner effect.

uses.use: Repairs damage from colour or heat
uses.note: Coats damaged areas temporarily.

safety: Very low risk.

name: Retinal (retinaldehyde)
summary: One conversion step from retinoic acid, so more potent than retinol. In a trial it reduced wrinkles alongside tretinoin, with less irritation.
what:
Retinaldehyde sits between retinol and retinoic acid in the skin's vitamin A pathway, so it needs only one step to become active. In a randomized trial, 0.05% retinaldehyde and 0.05% prescription retinoic acid both reduced wrinkles over 18 weeks compared with vehicle, and retinaldehyde caused less irritation.

It is less common than retinol because it is harder to stabilize, and product strengths (usually 0.05-0.1%) are often not shown.

evidence.summary: A randomized trial of 125 people with sun-damaged skin found 0.05% retinaldehyde and 0.05% retinoic acid both reduced wrinkles and roughness at 18 weeks versus vehicle, with retinaldehyde better tolerated. Earlier work showed dose-dependent retinoid activity in human skin at 0.05-0.5%. The evidence base is small.

uses.note: Reduced wrinkle and roughness measures versus vehicle at 18 weeks.
Caused less irritation than retinoic acid in the head-to-head trial, though it can still irritate.
Has retinoid and antibacterial activity, but few acne trials.

avoid_with: Strong exfoliating acids or benzoyl peroxide on the same night
safety: Avoid during pregnancy and while trying to conceive. Oral retinoids cause birth defects; a 2015 meta-analysis of about 650 exposed pregnancies found no clear rise in birth defects from topical retinoids, but it was too small to call them safe, so the standard advice is to stop.
Start a few nights a week; dryness and peeling are possible.
Use sunscreen by day.

studies.title: Profilometric evaluation of photodamage after topical retinaldehyde and retinoic acid treatment.
studies.authors: Creidi P, Vienne MP, Ochonisky S, Lauze C, Turlier V, Lagarde JM, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: 125 people with photodamaged faces used 0.05% retinaldehyde, 0.05% retinoic acid or vehicle; both actives reduced wrinkle and roughness measures at 18 weeks, and retinaldehyde was better tolerated.

studies.title: Topical retinaldehyde on human skin: biologic effects and tolerance.
studies.authors: Saurat JH, Didierjean L, Masgrau E, Piletta PA, Jaconi S, Chatellard-Gruaz D, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Retinaldehyde at 0.05-0.5% produced dose-dependent retinoid effects in human skin, such as a thicker epidermis and more cell turnover; in 229 patients, 0.05% and 0.1% preparations were well tolerated on the face for up to 3 years.

studies.title: Pregnancy outcomes following first-trimester exposure to topical retinoids: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Kaplan YC, Ozsarfati J, Etwel F, Nickel C, Nulman I, Koren G
studies.finding_summary: Across 654 pregnancies exposed to topical retinoids in the first trimester and 1,375 unexposed, there was no significant rise in major birth defects, miscarriage, low birthweight or prematurity; the authors call this reassuring after accidental exposure but too limited to justify using retinoids in pregnancy.

name: Retinol
summary: The strongest non-prescription retinoid for wrinkles. Skin converts it to retinoic acid; slower and gentler than prescription tretinoin, and not for pregnancy.
what:
Retinol is vitamin A. Skin converts it in two steps (retinol → retinaldehyde → retinoic acid) into the same molecule as prescription **tretinoin**, which switches on genes for collagen, faster cell turnover and a thicker epidermis. Only part of it is converted, so retinol is weaker than tretinoin but also less irritating.

Tretinoin is the benchmark: in a 1988 double-blind trial it improved photoaged facial skin in 14 of 15 people, while no vehicle-treated faces improved. Retinol's own evidence is smaller — in a 24-week trial a 0.4% lotion reduced fine wrinkles on the arms of elderly adults, with more collagen on biopsy. Expect results over 3-6 months, not weeks.

evidence.summary: Randomized, vehicle-controlled trials show retinol (about 0.1-1%) reduces fine wrinkles and raises collagen markers, though the studies are small and several are industry-funded. Prescription tretinoin has strong evidence from many large trials, and retinol produces similar but smaller changes in skin. Labels rarely state the percentage, which makes products hard to compare.

uses.note: 0.4% retinol improved fine wrinkling versus vehicle over 24 weeks; retinol causes the same kinds of skin changes as retinoic acid, only smaller.
Faster cell turnover smooths texture; the effect builds over months.
Prescription retinoids are first-line acne drugs; cosmetic retinol is weaker and much less studied for acne.
Helps uneven pigment gradually, mostly alongside sunscreen and other brighteners.
Retinol has to be converted in skin and is weaker; tretinoin remains the stronger option.

works_with: A plain moisturizer to buffer irritation
avoid_with: Strong AHA/BHA exfoliants or benzoyl peroxide on the same night — more irritation
Other retinoids — no benefit to stacking
safety: Avoid during pregnancy and while trying to conceive. Oral retinoids cause birth defects; a 2015 meta-analysis of about 650 exposed pregnancies found no clear rise in birth defects from topical retinoids, but it was too small to call them safe, so the standard advice is to stop.
Dryness, peeling and stinging are common in the first 2-6 weeks; start 2-3 nights a week and build up.
Apply at night and use sunscreen by day; retinoids can make skin more prone to sunburn.
Skip it on eczema-flared or broken skin, and stop before waxing, peels or laser unless a clinician says otherwise.

studies.title: Topical tretinoin improves photoaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled study.
studies.authors: Weiss JS, Ellis CN, Headington JT, Tincoff T, Hamilton TA, Voorhees JJ
studies.finding_summary: In a 16-week double-blind trial of prescription tretinoin, 14 of 15 patients treating the face improved versus none on vehicle, and all 30 improved on the tretinoin-treated forearm; irritation was the main side effect.

studies.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol).
studies.authors: Kafi R, Kwak HS, Schumacher WE, Cho S, Hanft VN, Hamilton TA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 36 elderly adults (mean age 87) had 0.4% retinol lotion applied to one arm and vehicle to the other for 24 weeks; retinol significantly reduced fine wrinkling and increased glycosaminoglycans and procollagen I on biopsy.

studies.title: A comparative study of the effects of retinol and retinoic acid on histological, molecular, and clinical properties of human skin.
studies.authors: Kong R, Cui Y, Fisher GJ, Wang X, Chen Y, Schneider LM, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Four weeks of retinol or retinoic acid both thickened the epidermis and raised collagen I and III expression, retinol to a smaller degree; 12 weeks of a retinol product reduced facial wrinkles on image analysis. Largely industry-authored.

studies.title: Pregnancy outcomes following first-trimester exposure to topical retinoids: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Kaplan YC, Ozsarfati J, Etwel F, Nickel C, Nulman I, Koren G
studies.finding_summary: Across 654 pregnancies exposed to topical retinoids in the first trimester and 1,375 unexposed, there was no significant rise in major birth defects, miscarriage, low birthweight or prematurity; the authors call this reassuring after accidental exposure but too limited to justify using retinoids in pregnancy.

name: Retinyl palmitate (vitamin A esters)
summary: The mildest vitamin A form. It needs three conversion steps to become active, so it is gentle but weak; mostly a label ingredient in lotions.
what:
Retinyl palmitate is retinol bound to a fatty acid — the form skin uses to store vitamin A. To act it must be cut back to retinol, then oxidized to retinaldehyde and retinoic acid. That makes it stable and non-irritating, and also much weaker: in a human-skin comparison it took about 0.6% retinyl palmitate under occlusion to match the effect of 0.025% retinol, and uncovered it performed worse.

It appears in body lotions, foot creams and eye creams, usually at unstated low levels. **Retinyl propionate** is a similar ester. A lotion that lists just "vitamin A" most often contains one of these esters, but the label doesn't say which.

evidence.summary: Human data are mostly penetration and skin-marker studies; controlled trials showing visible wrinkle improvement from retinyl palmitate alone are scarce. A mouse study raised concern that it might speed UV-induced tumours when used in sunscreen; a critical review judged that the data do not show a risk to people.

uses.note: So little is converted that effects, if any, are small.
The lotion's moisturizing base does most of this.

uses.use: Gentle vitamin A for sensitive skin
uses.note: Rarely irritates, precisely because so little becomes active.

safety: Most clinicians advise avoiding all retinoids, esters included, during pregnancy as a precaution, although absorption from a lotion is small.
Worries that retinyl palmitate in sunscreen causes skin cancer come from mouse data that reviewers consider not applicable to people.

studies.title: Unoccluded retinol penetrates human skin in vivo more effectively than unoccluded retinyl palmitate or retinoic acid.
studies.authors: Duell EA, Kang S, Voorhees JJ
studies.finding_summary: On human skin under occlusion, about 0.6% retinyl palmitate, 0.025% retinol and 0.01% retinaldehyde were needed to produce a measurable retinoid effect; without occlusion, retinyl palmitate did less well while retinol worked as well as when covered.

studies.title: Safety of retinyl palmitate in sunscreens: a critical analysis.
studies.authors: Wang SQ, Dusza SW, Lim HW
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Examined the mouse photocarcinogenicity data behind claims that retinyl palmitate in sunscreens promotes skin cancer, and concluded the evidence does not show such a risk in people.

name: Rosemary oil and extract
summary: Popular as 'natural minoxidil' on the strength of one small trial with no placebo group. Pleasant scent; hair-growth benefit unconfirmed.
what:
Rosemary essential oil is widely promoted for hair growth. The claim traces to a 2015 trial in which 100 people with pattern hair loss used rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil for 6 months: both groups gained some hair, with no difference between them.

That trial had no placebo arm, used low-strength minoxidil, and has not been independently repeated. Rosemary extracts in skin and body products are mostly there as antioxidants that protect the formula.

evidence.summary: One small randomised comparison without placebo found similar hair-count changes to 2% minoxidil at 6 months. Without a placebo group it cannot show that either did better than nothing, and it tested a leave-on oil, not a rinse-off shampoo.

uses.use: Regrows hair as well as minoxidil
uses.note: One small trial, no placebo, against the weaker 2% minoxidil.
Rinse-off contact is brief; the trial used a leave-on product.
A common and reasonable formulation use of rosemary extract.

typical: Essential oil usually under 1% in finished products; do not apply undiluted
safety: Undiluted essential oil can irritate or sensitise the scalp; patch-test leave-on products.
Keep essential oils away from eyes and out of reach of children.
For progressing hair loss, see a clinician: proven treatments exist and early treatment works best.

studies.title: Rosemary oil vs minoxidil 2% for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia: a randomized comparative trial.
studies.authors: Panahi Y, Taghizadeh M, Marzony ET, Sahebkar A
studies.finding_summary: 100 people with pattern hair loss used rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil for 6 months. Neither changed at 3 months; both had a significant rise in hair count at 6 months with no difference between groups, and scalp itch was more common with minoxidil.

name: Royal jelly
summary: A bee secretion marketed for hair growth and nourishment. There is no human evidence, and the one direct mouse study found it made hair thinner.
what: Royal jelly is the protein-rich secretion worker bees feed to queen larvae. Its 'queen bee' image drives claims that it nourishes hair and skin. In a 2025 study that tested it directly on hair growth, royal jelly applied to mouse skin produced thinner hair shafts and slowed hair follicle stem cells.

evidence.summary: No human trials support hair or skin benefits of topical royal jelly. The direct animal evidence (mice, 2025) points toward thinner hair, the opposite of the claim.

uses.note: No human trials; a mouse study found thinner hair shafts.
Any feel comes from the rest of the formula.

safety: Royal jelly can cause serious allergic reactions, including asthma attacks and anaphylaxis, mostly when swallowed; people with asthma, eczema or allergies to bees or pollen should avoid it.
Stop topical use if the scalp or skin becomes red, itchy or swollen.

studies.title: Royal Jelly Induces Thin Hair Shaft Formation by Suppressing Proliferation of Hair Follicle Stem Cells in Mice.
studies.authors: Hamanishi T, Koga H, Nishimura T, Kobayashi K
studies.finding_summary: Royal jelly applied to mouse skin produced thinner hair shafts and smaller hair bulbs, and suppressed hair follicle stem cell growth in mice and in culture: the opposite of the hair-growth claim.

name: Salicylic acid (BHA)
summary: An oil-soluble exfoliant that gets into pores. At 0.5-2% it is an approved over-the-counter acne ingredient with a modest but real benefit.
what:
Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid (BHA). Unlike AHAs it dissolves in oil, so it penetrates the sebum in pores and loosens the plug of cells behind blackheads and whiteheads. It is also mildly anti-inflammatory (it is chemically related to aspirin).

In the US it is an approved over-the-counter acne ingredient at 0.5-2%, and at higher strengths it treats dandruff, warts and calluses; clinic peels use 20-30%. In body lotions for rough, bumpy skin it works as a keratolytic, softening thick scale.

evidence.summary: It has long clinical use and a place in acne guidelines: the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline gives it a conditional recommendation (lower-certainty evidence), behind benzoyl peroxide and retinoids. A 2020 Cochrane review found only small, low-quality head-to-head trials. Peel studies support benefits for acne and sun damage.

uses.note: Its oil solubility suits clogged pores; the effect is modest.
Weaker than benzoyl peroxide or retinoids; best as one part of a routine.
Its keratolytic action softens thick scale and rough bumps.
An approved over-the-counter dandruff ingredient that loosens flakes.
Clearing debris can make pores look smaller; pore size is set mostly by genetics, age and oil output.

works_with: Benzoyl peroxide (alternate days if skin gets dry)
avoid_with: Layering other exfoliating acids and retinoids at the same time — irritation
safety: Salicylate poisoning (salicylism) from skin products is rare but reported, including deaths; the risk rises with high strengths, large areas, occlusion and use on children.
People allergic to aspirin should ask a clinician before using it.
In pregnancy, low-strength face products are generally considered acceptable; avoid high-strength peels and large-area body use.
Dryness and irritation are common with daily 2% use combined with other actives.

studies.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris.
studies.authors: Reynolds RV, Yeung H, Cheng CE, Cook-Bolden F, Desai SR, Druby KM, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: The American Academy of Dermatology's acne guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline, and conditional (lower-certainty) recommendations for topical salicylic acid, azelaic acid and clascoterone.

studies.title: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne.
studies.authors: Liu H, Yu H, Xia J, Liu L, Liu GJ, Sang H, Peinemann F
studies.finding_summary: 49 trials (3,880 people): azelaic acid is probably less effective than benzoyl peroxide and about as effective as tretinoin for acne; evidence for salicylic acid, nicotinamide and alpha-hydroxy acids was low or very low quality, from small head-to-head trials, and no conclusions were reported for zinc or sulphur.

studies.title: A review of toxicity from topical salicylic acid preparations.
studies.authors: Madan RK, Levitt J
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Reviews salicylic acid toxicity from skin products: salicylism, and even death, can occur from topical use, although it is rare; how much is absorbed depends on the vehicle and conditions of use.

studies.title: Salicylic acid as a peeling agent: a comprehensive review.
studies.authors: Arif T
studies.finding_summary: Reviews salicylic acid peels for acne, melasma, photodamage and freckles, including their documented efficacy and safety in both lighter and darker skin types, side effects and salicylism.

name: Silk proteins
summary: Proteins from silkworm silk that film the hair and hold moisture, adding softness and shine. A conditioning effect only.
what: Silk proteins (fibroin broken into amino acids or small peptides, and sericin, the silk 'gum') attract water and form a light film on the hair. The result is softer, glossier hair that combs more easily until the next wash.

evidence.summary: Support comes from ingredient-maker lab tests of gloss, moisture and combing. No trials show effects on hair growth or long-term hair health.

uses.note: Temporary conditioning effect.
Coating, not repair.

typical: Usually under 1% in shampoos, conditioners and styling products
safety: Very low risk; allergy to silk proteins is rare.

name: Sodium bicarbonate
summary: Baking soda: a very low-abrasion toothpaste cleaner that lifts stain and slightly reduces plaque and gum bleeding. In deodorants it neutralises odour but often irritates.
what:
In **toothpaste and mouthwash**, baking soda is a soft abrasive (pure baking soda has an RDA of about 7, far below silica) that still removes surface stain well, and it buffers plaque acids. It tastes salty, which is why some pastes are mostly baking soda and others use a little.

In **deodorants** it neutralises the acidic compounds that smell. It is alkaline, and a common reason 'natural' deodorants cause red, itchy or darkened underarms.

evidence.summary: A 2019 systematic review found baking soda pastes remove more plaque in single-brushing tests, only partly confirmed in longer trials, and slightly reduce gum bleeding. A network meta-analysis ranked it among the weaker toothpaste additives for gingivitis. Stain-removal evidence is good but comes from narrative reviews. The deodorant irritation point is from clinical experience, not trials.

uses.use: Removes surface stain with low wear
uses.note: Effective stain removal despite very low abrasivity.
Clear in single-use tests; small or inconsistent in longer trials.
Choose a baking soda paste that also contains fluoride.
Works chemically, but alkalinity irritates many people's skin.

typical: From a few percent up to over 60% in toothpaste; varies widely in deodorants
safety: Do not brush with neat kitchen baking soda as a substitute for toothpaste: you lose the fluoride.
If a baking soda deodorant causes redness, itching or darkening, stop using it; the rash usually settles, and a bicarbonate-free product avoids it.
People on strict sodium restriction need not worry about toothpaste: it is spat out.

studies.title: The efficacy of baking soda dentifrice in controlling plaque and gingivitis: A systematic review.
studies.authors: Valkenburg C, Kashmour Y, Dao A, Van der Weijden GA, Slot DE
studies.finding_summary: 21 publications: baking soda paste removed more plaque in single-brushing studies, only partly confirmed in longer studies; gum bleeding fell slightly versus control pastes, with no difference in gingival index. Moderate risk of bias, high heterogeneity.

studies.title: Stain removal and whitening by baking soda dentifrice: A review of literature.
studies.authors: Li Y
studies.finding_summary: In lab and clinical studies, baking soda toothpastes removed extrinsic stain effectively and safely despite relatively low abrasivity, in several studies better than more abrasive non-baking-soda pastes.

studies.title: Efficacy of adjunctive anti-plaque chemical agents in managing gingivitis: A systematic review and network meta-analyses.
studies.authors: Figuero E, Herrera D, Tobias A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 53 six-month trials. Among rinses, essential oils, chlorhexidine (0.10% or more) and cetylpyridinium chloride (above 0.05%) had the largest effects on gingivitis, with essential oils ranking highest; active toothpastes differed little from each other, with baking soda among the weakest.

name: Sodium fluoride
summary: The most common fluoride in toothpaste and mouthwash. Among the best-proven ingredients in any personal-care product: it cuts tooth decay by about a quarter.
what:
Fluoride makes enamel harder for acid to dissolve and helps early decay re-harden. Sodium fluoride is the simplest way to deliver it: most toothpastes carry about 1,000-1,450 ppm fluoride (0.22-0.32% sodium fluoride), and daily mouthwashes about 225 ppm (0.05%).

The benefit comes from fluoride sitting on the teeth, not from swallowing it. That is why the advice is to spit out the excess and not rinse straight after brushing.

evidence.summary: Decades of randomised trials, pooled in Cochrane reviews, show fluoride toothpaste prevents about 24% of decayed, missing and filled tooth surfaces in children, with a dose-response: 1,450-1,500 ppm does slightly better than 1,000-1,250 ppm. Adults benefit too. Fluoride rinses add protection in children. The main downside, dental fluorosis (white flecks in enamel), comes from young children swallowing toothpaste while their teeth are forming.

uses.note: High-certainty evidence from dozens of trials in children and adults.
1,450 ppm beats 1,000 ppm slightly; 5,000 ppm pastes are prescription products, mainly for high-risk adults.
Supervised rinsing cut decay about 27% in children; useful for people at high risk. Use it at a different time from brushing so you don't rinse the toothpaste fluoride away.

uses.use: Fluoride in toothpaste lowers children's IQ
uses.note: The IQ debate concerns drinking water above 1.5 mg/L (about twice the US target level), not toothpaste used as directed and spat out.

typical: Toothpaste 1,000-1,450 ppm fluoride (0.22-0.32% NaF; EU cosmetic maximum 1,500 ppm); daily rinse 0.05% NaF (about 225 ppm)
avoid_with: calcium carbonate as the abrasive (the calcium binds the fluoride in the tube, which is why chalk-based pastes use sodium monofluorophosphate instead)
safety: Children under 3: a smear the size of a grain of rice; ages 3-6: a pea-sized amount, with an adult supervising so they spit rather than swallow.
Dental fluorosis risk is from swallowing during tooth formation (under about age 6); the evidence linking toothpaste before 12 months to fluorosis is weak.
Swallowing a large amount (for example a child eating from the tube) can cause stomach upset or worse: call a poison control centre.
Prescription-strength pastes (up to 5,000 ppm) are for people a dentist has assessed as high-risk, mostly adults; do not use them for young children.

studies.title: Fluoride toothpastes of different concentrations for preventing dental caries.
studies.authors: Walsh T, Worthington HV, Glenny AM, Marinho VC, Jeroncic A
studies.finding_summary: 96 trials. High-to-moderate certainty that 1,000-1,250 ppm and 1,450-1,500 ppm fluoride toothpastes reduce caries in children and adolescents versus non-fluoride paste, with 1,450-1,500 ppm slightly better; 1,000-1,100 ppm also reduced decay in adults. Side effects were minimal where reported.

studies.title: Fluoride toothpastes for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents.
studies.authors: Marinho VC, Higgins JP, Sheiham A, Logan S
studies.finding_summary: Across 70 trials in 42,300 children, fluoride toothpaste prevented about 24% of decayed, missing and filled surfaces compared with non-fluoride paste; the effect was bigger with higher concentration, more frequent and supervised brushing.

studies.title: Topical fluoride as a cause of dental fluorosis in children.
studies.authors: Wong MC, Glenny AM, Tsang BW, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Mostly observational and at risk of bias: starting fluoride toothpaste before 12 months of age was weakly associated with more (mostly mild) fluorosis, and higher-fluoride pastes raised fluorosis risk in trials. Where fluorosis is a concern, under-6s may use pastes below 1,000 ppm.

studies.title: Fluoride mouthrinses for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents.
studies.authors: Marinho VC, Chong LY, Worthington HV, Walsh T
studies.finding_summary: 37 trials (15,813 children), mostly supervised school rinsing with sodium fluoride at 230 ppm daily or 900 ppm weekly: about 27% fewer decayed, missing and filled surfaces in permanent teeth (moderate-quality evidence).

name: Sodium monofluorophosphate
summary: A fluoride source that works in chalk-based toothpastes where sodium fluoride would be neutralised. Protects against decay about as well as sodium fluoride.
what:
Sodium monofluorophosphate holds its fluoride in a phosphate group that saliva enzymes release in the mouth. That lets it coexist with calcium-based abrasives such as calcium carbonate (chalk), which would lock up free sodium fluoride inside the tube.

A 0.76% concentration gives 1,000 ppm fluoride; 1.14% gives 1,500 ppm.

evidence.summary: Numerous clinical trials show SMFP toothpastes prevent decay. Head-to-head comparisons with sodium fluoride were long argued over; pooled analyses found no clinically meaningful difference. Those analyses were written largely by industry scientists, but the broader Cochrane evidence on fluoride toothpaste includes both.

uses.note: Equivalent to sodium fluoride at matched fluoride levels in pooled trials.
No meaningful difference; the choice is driven by which abrasive the paste uses.

safety: Children under 3: a smear the size of a grain of rice; ages 3-6: a pea-sized amount, with an adult supervising so they spit rather than swallow.
Same fluorosis and swallowing cautions as any fluoride toothpaste.

studies.title: The anti-caries efficacy of calcium carbonate-based fluoride toothpastes.
studies.authors: Lynch RJ, ten Cate JM
studies.finding_summary: Sodium monofluorophosphate in calcium carbonate toothpastes is an effective anti-caries combination in numerous clinical trials; the authors propose that calcium carbonate may add benefit by raising plaque calcium and neutralising acid, which is mechanistic and not separately proven.

studies.title: Clinical anticaries efficacy of NaF and SMFP dentifrices: overview and resolution of the scientific controversy.
studies.authors: Volpe AR, Petrone ME, Davies R, Proskin HM
studies.finding_summary: Re-analysing the head-to-head clinical trials, the authors found no statistically significant or clinically meaningful difference in caries prevention between sodium fluoride and sodium monofluorophosphate toothpastes.

name: Stannous fluoride
summary: A fluoride that also fights gum inflammation, sensitivity and acid erosion, thanks to the tin. Can stain teeth brown in some people.
what:
Stannous fluoride delivers the same anti-decay fluoride as sodium fluoride (about 1,100 ppm at the usual 0.454%), but the stannous (tin) ion adds three extras: it is antibacterial, it plugs the open tubules in exposed dentine that cause sensitivity, and it forms an acid-resistant layer that slows erosion from acidic drinks.

Older formulas stained teeth and tasted metallic; modern 'stabilised' versions reduce but do not always eliminate this.

evidence.summary: As a fluoride it prevents decay at least as well as other fluorides. Meta-analyses of six-month trials show a clinically meaningful reduction in gingivitis versus ordinary toothpaste, and network meta-analyses rank it among the most effective toothpaste ingredients for sensitivity. Many trials were run or funded by manufacturers, and results vary widely between studies.

uses.note: Similar or slightly better than other fluoride toothpastes.
Consistent but modest benefit over regular fluoride paste.
Moderate-to-high certainty in network meta-analyses; relief builds over 2-8 weeks of twice-daily use.
Better than other fluorides in 7 of 8 studies, though most were at high risk of bias.

safety: Can cause brown surface staining on teeth or tongue coating in some users; it polishes off at a cleaning and is less common with stabilised formulas.
Children under 3: a smear the size of a grain of rice; ages 3-6: a pea-sized amount, with an adult supervising so they spit rather than swallow.
Persistent sensitivity or bleeding gums need a dental check: they can signal decay, cracks or gum disease.

studies.title: A review of the effects of stannous fluoride on gingivitis.
studies.authors: Paraskevas S, van der Weijden GA
studies.finding_summary: 15 studies: stannous fluoride toothpastes reduced gingivitis compared with regular toothpaste, with less consistent effects on plaque; the size of the benefit was hard to pin down because results varied widely between studies.

studies.title: Stabilized stannous fluoride dentifrice in relation to dental caries, dental erosion and dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review.
studies.authors: Konradsson K, Lingstrom P, Emilson CG, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Stabilised stannous fluoride paste gave similar or slightly better caries protection than other fluoride pastes (few, high-bias studies), better protection against acid erosion in 7 of 8 studies, and less sensitivity in a meta-analysis of six 8-week trials.

studies.title: A meta-analysis of six-month studies of antiplaque and antigingivitis agents.
studies.authors: Gunsolley JC
studies.finding_summary: Six-month trials showed a clinically meaningful anti-gingivitis effect for stannous fluoride pastes, the largest body of support (21 studies) for essential-oil rinses, and variable results for cetylpyridinium chloride rinses depending on the formula. Unpublished manufacturer studies were included.

studies.title: Desensitizing Toothpastes for Dentin Hypersensitivity: A Network Meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Martins CC, Firmino RT, Riva JJ, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 125 RCTs (12,541 patients). Compared with ordinary fluoride paste, stannous fluoride, potassium salts (alone or combined with stannous fluoride), calcium sodium phosphosilicate, arginine and strontium reduced sensitivity to at least one stimulus, with moderate-to-high certainty.

name: Stevia
summary: A plant-based sweetener used in some 'natural' toothpastes. It makes the paste palatable without feeding decay bacteria; it has no oral-health effect of its own.
what: Stevia extracts are intensely sweet compounds from the stevia plant. In toothpaste they replace sweeteners such as saccharin, usually as part of a 'natural' positioning. Like other non-sugar sweeteners, mouth bacteria cannot ferment them into acid.

evidence.summary: There is no clinical evidence that stevia in toothpaste improves oral health. Its only role is taste, and toothpastes do not contain sugar anyway.

uses.note: Not fermented by decay-causing bacteria.
Some lab studies only; no clinical trials in toothpaste.

safety: Very well tolerated; allergy is rare.
A 'natural' sweetened paste still needs fluoride to protect against decay; check the label.

name: Tea tree oil
summary: An antimicrobial essential oil. 5% gels helped mild acne and a 5% shampoo helped dandruff in trials, but it's a common allergen, especially once oxidized.
what:
Tea tree oil is distilled from the leaves of an Australian tree. Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, kills bacteria and yeasts in the lab, including the acne bacterium and the yeast linked to dandruff. It turns up in acne gels, shampoos, body washes and some toothpastes.

The trials used 5%; many products contain far less or don't say. Neat oil irritates skin and is toxic if swallowed.

evidence.summary: Small randomized trials support 5% tea tree oil for mild to moderate acne (better than placebo; slower than 5% benzoyl peroxide but with fewer side effects) and for dandruff (41% vs 11% improvement with placebo over 4 weeks). Trials are small and short, and contact allergy is well documented.

uses.note: 5% gel beat placebo in one trial and worked more slowly but more gently than 5% benzoyl peroxide in another.
A 5% shampoo improved dandruff severity 41% vs 11% with placebo over 4 weeks.
Too little oil and too few trials to tell.

safety: A common cause of allergic contact dermatitis; oxidized (old, air-exposed) oil is more allergenic, so keep bottles capped and discard old oil.
Never apply undiluted oil or swallow it; ingestion has caused serious poisoning, especially in children.

Case reports linked repeated use of lavender and tea tree products to breast growth in young boys that reversed after stopping; causation is debated, but limiting use in prepubertal children is a cautious choice.

studies.title: A comparative study of tea-tree oil versus benzoylperoxide in the treatment of acne.
studies.authors: Bassett IB, Pannowitz DL, Barnetson RS
studies.finding_summary: 124 patients with mild to moderate acne used 5% tea tree oil gel or 5% benzoyl peroxide lotion; both reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesions, tea tree oil more slowly but with fewer side effects.

studies.title: The efficacy of 5% topical tea tree oil gel in mild to moderate acne vulgaris: a randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled study.
studies.authors: Enshaieh S, Jooya A, Siadat AH, Iraji F
studies.journal: Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology
studies.finding_summary: 60 patients with mild to moderate acne used 5% tea tree oil gel or placebo for 45 days; tea tree oil was 3.55 times more effective on total lesion count and 5.75 times on severity, with similar, tolerable side effects.

studies.title: Treatment of dandruff with 5% tea tree oil shampoo.
studies.authors: Satchell AC, Saurajen A, Bell C, Barnetson RS
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: 126 people with mild to moderate dandruff used 5% tea tree oil shampoo or placebo daily for 4 weeks; severity scores improved 41% versus 11%, with no adverse effects.

studies.title: Prepubertal gynecomastia linked to lavender and tea tree oils.
studies.authors: Henley DV, Lipson N, Korach KS, Bloch CA
studies.finding_summary: Three prepubertal boys developed breast enlargement while using products containing lavender and tea tree oils; it resolved after they stopped, and both oils showed weak estrogenic and anti-androgenic activity in human cell lines. Causation was disputed in later correspondence.

studies.title: Tea tree oil: contact allergy and chemical composition.
studies.authors: de Groot AC, Schmidt E
studies.finding_summary: Tea tree oil has caused more published allergic reactions than any other essential oil; 0.1-3.5% of people patch-tested react. Fresh oil is a weak-to-moderate sensitiser, but oxidised (old, air-exposed) oil is much stronger. Most cases come from neat oil, a minority from cosmetics.

name: Thymol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate
summary: The fixed essential-oil blend in classic antiseptic mouthwash. Well-tested as an add-on to brushing for plaque and gingivitis; poisonous if a child drinks it.
what:
These three plant-derived compounds (thymol from thyme, eucalyptol from eucalyptus, methyl salicylate, the main part of wintergreen oil) are combined with menthol at fixed low levels (about 0.04-0.09% each) in the classic antiseptic mouthwash. Together they disrupt the bacterial film on teeth and gums.

The evidence is for the combination as a rinse, not for any one of these compounds alone. Classic versions contain roughly 20-27% alcohol; alcohol-free versions exist.

evidence.summary: A meta-analysis of 29 six-month placebo-controlled trials found the rinse, added to brushing and flossing, reduced gingivitis by about 16% and plaque by about 28%; all trials were industry-sponsored. Independent systematic reviews agree: in a network meta-analysis it ranked highest among rinses for gingivitis, and it matched chlorhexidine for gum inflammation over the long term, though chlorhexidine controls plaque better.

uses.note: Consistent benefit across many six-month trials; the size is modest.
Short-term freshness is obvious; lasting improvement has low-certainty evidence.

uses.use: Alcohol in the rinse causes mouth cancer
uses.note: Studies conflict; no causal link has been established. Alcohol-free versions avoid the question and the sting.

typical: Thymol about 0.064%, eucalyptol about 0.092%, methyl salicylate about 0.060% (with menthol about 0.042%)
safety: Keep out of reach of children: swallowing a large amount is dangerous because of the alcohol and the salicylate (related to aspirin). Pure wintergreen oil is highly toxic even in small amounts.
Follow the age limit on the label; young children cannot reliably spit.
People avoiding alcohol (recovery, certain medications, religious reasons) should choose an alcohol-free version.
The sting and a temporary taste change are common; stop if the mouth becomes sore or ulcerated.

studies.title: Meta-analysis of the effect of an essential oil-containing mouthrinse on gingivitis and plaque.
studies.authors: Araujo MWB, Charles CA, Weinstein RB, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 29 six-month, placebo-controlled trials: adding an essential-oil rinse to brushing and flossing reduced whole-mouth gingivitis by about 16% and plaque by about 28%; 45% of rinse users versus 14% of controls had at least half their gum sites healthy.

studies.title: Efficacy of adjunctive anti-plaque chemical agents in managing gingivitis: A systematic review and network meta-analyses.
studies.authors: Figuero E, Herrera D, Tobias A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 53 six-month trials.
