Among rinses, essential oils, chlorhexidine (0.10% or more) and cetylpyridinium chloride (above 0.05%) had the largest effects on gingivitis, with essential oils ranking highest; active toothpastes differed little from each other, with baking soda among the weakest.

studies.title: Essential oils compared to chlorhexidine with respect to plaque and parameters of gingival inflammation: a systematic review.
studies.authors: Van Leeuwen MP, Slot DE, Van der Weijden GA
studies.finding_summary: 19 studies: over 4 weeks or more, chlorhexidine controlled plaque better, but the essential-oil rinse matched it for reducing gum inflammation, making it a reasonable long-term alternative.

studies.title: A meta-analysis of six-month studies of antiplaque and antigingivitis agents.
studies.authors: Gunsolley JC
studies.finding_summary: Six-month trials showed a clinically meaningful anti-gingivitis effect for stannous fluoride pastes, the largest body of support (21 studies) for essential-oil rinses, and variable results for cetylpyridinium chloride rinses depending on the formula. Unpublished manufacturer studies were included.

name: Titanium dioxide
summary: Mineral UV filter in sunscreens and a white pigment in toothpaste. Strong on UVB, weaker in long-wave UVA; the concerns are about inhaling or swallowing it, not skin contact.
what:
Titanium dioxide does two jobs in this catalogue. In **sunscreens** it is a mineral UV filter: very effective against UVB and short-wave UVA, less so against long-wave UVA1, so it is usually paired with zinc oxide or an organic UVA filter. Like zinc oxide it is photostable and rarely causes allergy.

In **toothpaste** it is simply a white colourant (listed as CI 77891) that makes the paste look bright. It does not whiten teeth.

evidence.summary: As a sunscreen filter its protection is measured directly in SPF testing, and it is one of the three filters the FDA currently regards as safe and effective. Safety questions concern other routes: EFSA concluded in 2021 that swallowed particles could not be ruled out as genotoxic, which ended its use as a food additive in the EU, and inhaled fine powder is classed as a possible carcinogen based on rat studies. Neither is a finding of harm from use on skin.

uses.note: Strong UVB and UVA2 blocker; needs a partner filter for full UVA1 coverage.
It only colours the paste. Whitening in toothpaste comes from abrasives or peroxide.

The EU banned it in food in 2022 after EFSA could not exclude genotoxicity. In 2024 the EU's cosmetics committee said the data could not rule this out for most grades used in oral products either; it remains permitted in toothpaste while more data are reviewed.

typical: Up to 25% as a sunscreen filter (US and EU); small amounts as a pigment in toothpaste
safety: Avoid inhaling powders and sprays; in the EU, nano titanium dioxide is not allowed in products that could be inhaled, and fine powder is classed as a suspected carcinogen by inhalation.
Toothpaste: children swallow more, so use the recommended amount (a smear under 3, pea-sized from 3 to 6). If you would rather avoid swallowed titanium dioxide, pigment-free pastes exist.
Allergy is very rare.

studies.title: Safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171) as a food additive.
studies.authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF), Younes M, Aquilina G, et al.
studies.finding_summary: EFSA found no organ or reproductive toxicity at high doses, but could not rule out that swallowed titanium dioxide particles damage DNA, and concluded it could no longer be considered safe as a food additive. This led to the EU food ban; it is not a finding about skin use.

name: Tranexamic acid
summary: A bleeding drug repurposed for melasma and dark spots. Topical 2-5% shows promise in small trials; the oral prescription form is better studied.
what:
Tranexamic acid blocks plasmin, an enzyme that in skin helps UV light and hormones switch on pigment cells and new blood vessels. Low-dose oral tranexamic acid is a recognized off-label prescription treatment for melasma.

Topical versions at 2-5% avoid the systemic clotting concerns. In small trials they reduced melasma, including a split-face trial where 3% tranexamic acid matched hydroquinone plus a steroid, with fewer side effects. Results take 8-12 weeks, and melasma returns without ongoing sun protection.

evidence.summary: A handful of small trials (about 20-50 people, 12 weeks) show topical 2-3% tranexamic acid reduces melasma severity; one double-blind split-face trial found it comparable to 3% hydroquinone with dexamethasone. A 2017 review concluded efficacy is not yet adequately established. Evidence for other dark spots, such as sun spots and post-acne marks, is thinner.

uses.note: Small trials are positive; the oral form has stronger evidence than the topical.
Plausible, but few trials outside melasma.

works_with: Daily sunscreen — tinted formulas with iron oxides also block visible light that worsens melasma
safety: Topical use is well tolerated; mild irritation is the usual side effect.
Oral tranexamic acid is a different product with clotting risks; it needs a prescription and isn't for people with a history of blood clots.

studies.title: Topical tranexamic acid as a promising treatment for melasma.
studies.authors: Ebrahimi B, Naeini FF
studies.journal: Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
studies.finding_summary: 50 Iranian women with melasma applied 3% tranexamic acid to one side of the face and 3% hydroquinone + 0.01% dexamethasone to the other for 12 weeks; both improved similarly, with significantly fewer side effects on the tranexamic acid side.

studies.title: Efficacy and possible mechanisms of topical tranexamic acid in melasma.
studies.authors: Kim SJ, Park JY, Shibata T, Fujiwara R, Kang HY
studies.finding_summary: 23 people with mostly mild melasma applied 2% tranexamic acid for 12 weeks; melasma scores improved in 22, and biopsies showed less epidermal melanin and lower endothelin-1. No control group; one author was from a cosmetics company.

studies.title: Tranexamic acid in treatment of melasma: A comprehensive review of clinical studies.
studies.authors: Taraz M, Niknam S, Ehsani AH
studies.finding_summary: Reviews oral, topical and injected tranexamic acid for melasma and concludes that its efficacy is not yet adequately established; more studies are needed.

name: Turmeric extract
summary: A spice extract whose curcumin is anti-inflammatory in the lab. Evidence on skin is early and small, and it can stain skin yellow.
what:
Turmeric root contains curcumin, a yellow polyphenol with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies. In skincare it appears in brightening and calming serums and masks.

Curcumin dissolves poorly and breaks down easily, and products rarely say how much they contain. Strongly coloured products can leave a yellow tint on skin and fabric.

evidence.summary: A 2016 systematic review found 18 small clinical studies of oral or topical turmeric or curcumin across acne, psoriasis, photoaging and other conditions; 10 reported significant improvement, but the authors called the evidence early and limited. Few studies test cosmetic topical products.

uses.note: Lab evidence and a few small studies.
Not well tested in skincare products.
Early, small studies only.

safety: Can cause allergic contact dermatitis, reported more often as turmeric products have become popular.
May temporarily stain skin yellow-orange.

studies.title: Effects of Turmeric (Curcuma longa) on Skin Health: A Systematic Review of the Clinical Evidence.
studies.authors: Vaughn AR, Branum A, Sivamani RK
studies.finding_summary: Of 18 clinical studies of oral or topical turmeric/curcumin across skin conditions, 10 reported statistically significant improvement over control, but the studies were limited and further research is needed.

name: Vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid)
summary: The topical antioxidant with the best evidence, if the formula is right: pure L-ascorbic acid at 10-20% and below pH 3.5, protected from air and light.
what:
L-ascorbic acid is the active form of vitamin C. In skin it neutralizes free radicals made by UV and pollution, is a required cofactor for building collagen, and slows melanin production. The catch is chemistry: it is unstable in water, turns yellow-brown as it oxidizes, and only crosses the skin's outer layer when the product is acidic.

The key absorption work (Pinnell 2001, on pig skin) found L-ascorbic acid entered skin only at **pH below 3.5**, absorption rose up to about **20%** and not beyond, and skin levels stayed up for days after stopping. A label that just says "vitamin C" may mean pure ascorbic acid or a derivative, so check the ingredient list.

evidence.summary: Small randomized, vehicle-controlled trials (about 20-40 people, 3-6 months) found 5-10% vitamin C creams improved fine lines, roughness and tone in sun-damaged skin, and lab studies show it reduces UV damage markers. Trials are small and formulations vary widely, so one product's results don't transfer to another. It absorbs almost no UV, so it is not a sunscreen.

uses.use: Fine lines and texture from sun damage
uses.note: A 6-month double-blind trial of 5% vitamin C cream found better skin texture and fewer deep furrows than its base cream, with elastic-fibre repair on biopsy.
Slows melanin production; brightening builds over weeks to months.
Reduces UV-induced redness and damage markers, especially with vitamin E and ferulic acid, but gives no meaningful SPF. Always pair with sunscreen.
Required for collagen building and shown to increase it in lab and biopsy work; visible firming in people is modest.
Some small trials show lightening, but it is weaker than dedicated pigment treatments such as azelaic acid or tranexamic acid.

works_with: Vitamin E and ferulic acid — they stabilize it and doubled its UV protection in lab tests
avoid_with: Strong acid exfoliants or retinoids in the same step if your skin stings — use vitamin C in the morning and the others at night
safety: The low pH means stinging and redness are common at first; start every other day or with a lower strength.
A serum that has turned dark orange or brown has oxidized and lost much of its activity, and can leave a temporary yellow-orange tint on skin.

studies.title: Topical L-ascorbic acid: percutaneous absorption studies.
studies.authors: Pinnell SR, Yang H, Omar M, Monteiro-Riviere N, DeBuys HV, Walker LC, et al.
studies.finding_summary: L-ascorbic acid entered pig skin only when formulated below pH 3.5, with absorption maximal at 20%; skin levels saturated after three daily applications and fell with a half-life of about 4 days. Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate and dehydroascorbic acid did not raise skin vitamin C levels.

studies.title: Topical ascorbic acid on photoaged skin. Clinical, topographical and ultrastructural evaluation: double-blind study vs. placebo.
studies.authors: Humbert PG, Haftek M, Creidi P, Lapière C, Nusgens B, Richard A, et al.
studies.finding_summary: In a 6-month double-blind trial on the neck and arms of women with photoaged skin, 5% vitamin C cream improved clinical scores, skin microrelief and deep furrows versus its base cream, with biopsy evidence of elastic tissue repair.

studies.title: Topical Vitamin C and the Skin: Mechanisms of Action and Clinical Applications.
studies.authors: Al-Niaimi F, Chiang NYZ
studies.journal: Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Reviews topical vitamin C's antioxidant, photoprotective, collagen-supporting and anti-pigment actions, and concludes that clinical efficacy studies remain limited, with stability and penetration the main formulation challenges.

studies.title: Ferulic acid stabilizes a solution of vitamins C and E and doubles its photoprotection of skin.
studies.authors: Lin FH, Lin JY, Gupta RD, Tournas JA, Burch JA, Selim MA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Adding ferulic acid to a 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol solution improved its chemical stability and doubled its protection of skin against solar-simulated UV (from about 4-fold to about 8-fold), measured by redness and sunburn cells; thymine dimer formation was also reduced.

name: Vitamin C derivatives
summary: Stable, gentler forms of vitamin C that don't brown or sting, but must be converted in skin and have far less evidence than pure ascorbic acid.
what:
Because L-ascorbic acid is fragile and needs a very acidic formula, chemists attach it to a sugar (**ascorbyl glucoside**), a phosphate (**sodium or magnesium ascorbyl phosphate**) or a fatty acid (**ascorbyl palmitate**). These keep longer, work at a skin-friendly pH and rarely sting.

The trade-off is delivery: enzymes in skin must cut them back to ascorbic acid, and how much gets through is uncertain. In the pig-skin study that set the rules for vitamin C serums, magnesium ascorbyl phosphate and ascorbyl palmitate did not raise skin vitamin C levels at all. Ascorbyl palmitate is mostly used to protect a formula's oils.

evidence.summary: Evidence is mostly lab work plus a few small clinical studies, often run by ingredient makers and without placebo groups: a 10% magnesium ascorbyl phosphate cream lightened spots in about half of patients with melasma or age spots, and a 5% sodium ascorbyl phosphate lotion was reported to help acne in an open study. There are almost no head-to-head trials against L-ascorbic acid.

uses.note: A 10% magnesium ascorbyl phosphate cream lightened spots in 19 of 34 patients in an older study; ascorbyl glucoside is widely used for this but has little independent trial data.
Sodium ascorbyl phosphate kills acne bacteria in the lab and a 5% lotion helped in an open, manufacturer-run study without placebo.

uses.use: Works as well as pure vitamin C
uses.note: Pure L-ascorbic acid has the stronger evidence; in the key absorption study two derivatives didn't raise skin vitamin C levels.
They work near skin's normal pH, so stinging is uncommon.

safety: Well tolerated; irritation is much less common than with pure ascorbic acid.

studies.title: Topical L-ascorbic acid: percutaneous absorption studies.
studies.authors: Pinnell SR, Yang H, Omar M, Monteiro-Riviere N, DeBuys HV, Walker LC, et al.
studies.finding_summary: L-ascorbic acid entered pig skin only when formulated below pH 3.5, with absorption maximal at 20%; skin levels saturated after three daily applications and fell with a half-life of about 4 days. Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate and dehydroascorbic acid did not raise skin vitamin C levels.

studies.title: Inhibitory effect of magnesium L-ascorbyl-2-phosphate (VC-PMG) on melanogenesis in vitro and in vivo.
studies.authors: Kameyama K, Sakai C, Kondoh S, Yonemoto K, Nishiyama S, Tagawa M, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
studies.finding_summary: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate inhibited melanin formation in lab tests and reached the epidermis; a 10% cream produced significant lightening in 19 of 34 patients with melasma or age spots and in 3 of 25 with normal skin.

studies.title: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate shows in vitro and in vivo efficacy in the prevention and treatment of acne vulgaris.
studies.authors: Klock J, Ikeno H, Ohmori K, Nishikawa T, Vollhardt J, Schehlmann V
studies.finding_summary: From the ingredient's manufacturer: 1% sodium ascorbyl phosphate killed acne bacteria in the lab, a formula with it reduced UVA-induced sebum oxidation in 20 people, and a 5% lotion was rated excellent or good in 77% of 60 people with acne in an open 12-week study.

name: Vitamin E (tocopherol)
summary: A fat-soluble antioxidant that mostly keeps a formula's oils fresh. It helps vitamin C protect skin, but on scars it doesn't help and often causes a rash.
what:
Vitamin E is a family of fat-soluble antioxidants. **Tocopherol** is the active form; **tocopheryl acetate** is a more stable ester that skin has to convert, and it does so only slowly. On most labels it sits at well under 1%, where its job is to stop the product's plant oils going rancid — useful, but a job for the bottle rather than your skin.

Its clearest role on skin is as a partner: applied with vitamin C (and ferulic acid) it adds to protection against UV-triggered redness and damage. On its own, the popular uses — fading scars, healing wounds, preventing stretch marks — have not held up in trials.

evidence.summary: Lab and small human studies show tocopherol reaches the skin and, combined with vitamin C, reduces UV-induced redness and sunburn cells. Controlled evidence that vitamin E alone improves wrinkles or scars is thin, and a small double-blind scar trial found no benefit and frequent allergic reactions. None of this makes vitamin E a sunscreen.

uses.note: In a double-blind trial on surgical scars, vitamin E did nothing or made the scar look worse in 90% of cases, and a third of patients developed a rash.
A 15% vitamin C + 1% vitamin E serum reduced UV-induced redness and sunburn cells; adding ferulic acid doubled that. It adds to sunscreen, it doesn't replace it.
Vitamin E oils soften skin mainly because they are oils; there is little evidence tocopherol itself adds hydration.
No good trial shows vitamin E prevents or fades stretch marks.
Its most reliable job: it slows oxidation of the plant oils in a formula.

works_with: Vitamin C and ferulic acid — the combination with the best evidence
safety: Allergic contact dermatitis is uncommon given how widely vitamin E is used, but it happens; stop a new product that itches or causes a rash.
Don't apply vitamin E to fresh surgical wounds or scars — the one controlled trial found more harm than benefit.

studies.title: The effects of topical vitamin E on the cosmetic appearance of scars.
studies.authors: Baumann LS, Spencer J
studies.finding_summary: 15 patients applied a plain emollient to one half of a surgical scar and the same emollient with vitamin E to the other half for 4 weeks; vitamin E had no effect or worsened appearance in 90% of cases, and 33% developed contact dermatitis.

studies.title: Vitamin E and allergic contact dermatitis.
studies.authors: Kosari P, Alikhan A, Sockolov M, Feldman SR
studies.finding_summary: A literature search found 931 reported cases of vitamin E allergic contact dermatitis, mostly from one large study; the authors judged it uncommon relative to how widely vitamin E is used in skin care.

studies.title: Ferulic acid stabilizes a solution of vitamins C and E and doubles its photoprotection of skin.
studies.authors: Lin FH, Lin JY, Gupta RD, Tournas JA, Burch JA, Selim MA, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Adding ferulic acid to a 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol solution improved its chemical stability and doubled its protection of skin against solar-simulated UV (from about 4-fold to about 8-fold), measured by redness and sunburn cells; thymine dimer formation was also reduced.

name: Willow bark extract
summary: A plant extract sold as 'natural BHA'. Its salicin is not meaningfully converted to salicylic acid in skin; expect a mild soothing extract, not an acne treatment.
what:
Willow bark contains salicin and other salicylates plus polyphenols. Salicin becomes salicylic acid in the gut and liver when you swallow it, but there is little evidence skin converts it to any useful degree, so a willow bark 'BHA' is not equivalent to salicylic acid.

In formulas it adds mild anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity seen in cell studies.

evidence.summary: Evidence is limited to cell and lab studies showing anti-inflammatory effects, plus small manufacturer-run studies of salicin products. No controlled trials show willow bark extract clears acne or exfoliates like salicylic acid.

uses.note: Contains salicin, but there is no good evidence skin turns it into salicylic acid or that it matches salicylic acid's effect.
Anti-inflammatory in cell studies only.

safety: People with aspirin or salicylate allergy should be cautious.
Plant extracts can cause contact allergy; patch test if your skin is reactive.

name: Zinc citrate
summary: Zinc in toothpaste slows tartar build-up and plaque bacteria and binds bad-breath compounds. Modest benefits; doesn't interfere with fluoride.
what: Zinc ions stick to teeth and plaque for hours. They slow bacterial growth, bind the sulfur compounds behind bad breath, and interfere with the mineral crystals that turn plaque into hard tartar (calculus). Zinc citrate is the usual form in toothpaste, often with fluoride and sometimes stannous fluoride.

evidence.summary: Industry-run clinical trials show zinc pastes reduce new tartar formation and plaque, and zinc does not blunt fluoride's anti-decay effect. Evidence on bad breath is low certainty. A meta-analysis of six-month trials found no anti-gingivitis benefit for older pastes combining zinc citrate with triclosan. Existing tartar needs professional cleaning.

uses.note: Reduces new tartar; does not remove existing tartar.
Mechanism is sound; clinical evidence is limited and short-term.
Small plaque effects; not a treatment for gum disease.

safety: Can leave a slight metallic or astringent taste.
Children under 3: a smear the size of a grain of rice; ages 3-6: a pea-sized amount, with an adult supervising so they spit rather than swallow.

studies.title: Zinc in the mouth, its interactions with dental enamel and possible effects on caries; a review of the literature.
studies.authors: Lynch RJ
studies.finding_summary: Zinc is added to toothpastes and rinses to control plaque, bad breath and tartar and persists in the mouth for hours. In caries trials, adding zinc to fluoride toothpaste did not reduce fluoride's anti-caries effect.

studies.title: A meta-analysis of six-month studies of antiplaque and antigingivitis agents.
studies.authors: Gunsolley JC
studies.finding_summary: Six-month trials showed a clinically meaningful anti-gingivitis effect for stannous fluoride pastes, the largest body of support (21 studies) for essential-oil rinses, and variable results for cetylpyridinium chloride rinses depending on the formula. Unpublished manufacturer studies were included.

name: Zinc oxide
summary: A mineral filter covering UVB and UVA, including long-wave UVA1. Photostable, rarely allergenic, and one of only three filters the FDA currently calls safe and effective.
what:
Zinc oxide is a white mineral powder that absorbs (and to a lesser extent scatters) ultraviolet light. Alone it covers UVB through long-wave UVA1 up to about 380 nm, which few single filters manage, and it does not break down in sunlight.

The trade-off is a white cast. Smaller ("nano" or "micronised") particles reduce the cast; coated grades keep the particles from reacting with the rest of the formula. The same ingredient is the active in many nappy-rash and skin-protectant creams.

evidence.summary: Zinc oxide's UV protection is measured directly in standard SPF and UVA tests, and sunscreens as a class reduce sunburn, squamous-cell skin cancer and photoageing in randomised trials. Volunteer studies show the particles stay on the surface of intact skin; a trace of dissolved zinc is absorbed, which is trivial next to dietary zinc. What is not shown: that mineral sunscreens protect better than a well-formulated chemical one at the same SPF and UVA rating.

uses.note: One of the few single filters that reaches into UVA1; the SPF and 'broad spectrum' labels are what confirm the finished product works.

uses.use: Suitable for sensitive or allergy-prone skin and children
uses.note: Allergy to zinc oxide is very rare, which is why dermatologists often suggest mineral filters for reactive skin and young children.

uses.use: Nanoparticles get through the skin into the body
uses.note: Repeated-application volunteer studies found particles stayed on the skin surface; only tiny amounts of dissolved zinc were absorbed.
Some lab studies show zinc oxide particles can harm corals too; 'reef safe' is not a regulated claim.

typical: Up to 25% (US and EU maximum); often 10-25% as the sole filter
safety: Avoid inhaling it: prefer lotions over loose powders and sprays, particularly for children. In the EU, nano zinc oxide is not allowed in products that could be inhaled.
Babies under 6 months: shade and clothing first; ask a clinician before routine sunscreen use.
A white cast can tempt people to apply less; SPF is tested at about 2 mg/cm2, and thin layers give far less protection.

studies.title: Support for the Safe Use of Zinc Oxide Nanoparticle Sunscreens: Lack of Skin Penetration or Cellular Toxicity after Repeated Application in Volunteers.
studies.authors: Mohammed YH, Holmes A, Haridass IN, et al.
studies.finding_summary: Zinc oxide nanoparticles applied repeatedly for 5 days stayed on the skin surface and in skin furrows and did not enter or harm the living epidermis; a small amount of dissolved zinc ion penetrated without local toxicity.

studies.title: Small amounts of zinc from zinc oxide particles in sunscreens applied outdoors are absorbed through human skin.
studies.authors: Gulson B, McCall M, Korsch M, et al.
studies.finding_summary: 20 adults used isotope-labelled zinc oxide sunscreen outdoors for 5 days. The overwhelming majority of zinc was not absorbed; tracer in blood was about 1/1000 of the body's normal blood zinc. Whether it crossed as particles or dissolved zinc was not known.

name: Zinc PCA
summary: Zinc bound to a natural moisturizing molecule, sold for oily and blemish-prone skin. Topical zinc's acne evidence is modest and mostly in combinations.
what:
Zinc PCA pairs zinc with PCA (pyrrolidone carboxylic acid), part of the skin's own natural moisturizing factor. Zinc has mild antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects and may reduce oil production in lab studies, so zinc PCA is sold for oil control and blemishes, usually at low levels.

Most clinical evidence for zinc in acne involves zinc taken by mouth or zinc combined with a prescription antibiotic, not zinc PCA on its own.

evidence.summary: Reviews support zinc's anti-inflammatory role in acne, largely from oral and combination treatments. A 2020 Cochrane review set out to assess topical zinc for acne but reported no conclusive findings for it, and specific trials of zinc PCA are small and often manufacturer-run.

uses.note: Sebum-reducing effects are mostly from lab and small studies.
Zinc helps as an add-on in some studies; on its own the evidence is weak.

safety: Well tolerated.

studies.title: Zinc therapy in dermatology: a review.
studies.authors: Gupta M, Mahajan VK, Mehta KS, Chauhan PS
studies.finding_summary: Reviews oral and topical zinc across skin conditions, including acne, rosacea, melasma and infections, and topical zinc salts as soothing, photoprotective and anti-dandruff agents.

studies.title: Topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and fruit acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) for acne.
studies.authors: Liu H, Yu H, Xia J, Liu L, Liu GJ, Sang H, Peinemann F
studies.finding_summary: 49 trials (3,880 people): azelaic acid is probably less effective than benzoyl peroxide and about as effective as tretinoin for acne; evidence for salicylic acid, nicotinamide and alpha-hydroxy acids was low or very low quality, from small head-to-head trials, and no conclusions were reported for zinc or sulphur.

name: Zinc pyrithione
summary: The long-standing anti-dandruff drug in US shampoos. Works well against the yeast behind dandruff, but has been banned in EU cosmetics since 2022.
what:
Zinc pyrithione kills Malassezia, the scalp yeast that drives dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis. In the US it is an approved over-the-counter dandruff active: 0.3-2% in rinse-off shampoos and 0.1-0.25% in leave-on products.

The EU banned it from all cosmetics in March 2022 after it was classified as toxic to reproduction (based on animal data), even though the EU's safety committee had judged shampoos up to 1% safe. European anti-dandruff shampoos now mostly use piroctone olamine or climbazole instead.

evidence.summary: Decades of randomised trials show zinc pyrithione shampoos reduce dandruff; in a 331-person trial, 1% zinc pyrithione improved severe dandruff by 67% at 4 weeks versus 73% for 2% ketoconazole, which also had fewer relapses. The EU ban reflects a hazard classification from animal studies, not observed harm to shampoo users.

uses.note: Effective with regular use, 2-3 times a week or more; flakes return when you stop.

uses.use: Treats seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp
uses.note: Helps mild cases; ketoconazole is somewhat stronger.
Dandruff control is not a hair-loss treatment.

typical: 0.3-2% in rinse-off shampoo (US; often 1%); banned in EU cosmetics
safety: Leave the lather on the scalp for a few minutes before rinsing; keep it out of the eyes.
Stop if the scalp becomes irritated. See a clinician if flaking is thick, red, or spreads to the face or body, or if a medicated shampoo has not helped after a few weeks.
Pregnant people who want to minimise exposure can choose another dandruff active; this is a precaution based on animal data, not evidence of harm from shampoo.

studies.title: A multicenter randomized trial of ketoconazole 2% and zinc pyrithione 1% shampoos in severe dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.
studies.authors: Pierard-Franchimont C, Goffin V, Decroix J, Pierard GE
studies.finding_summary: 331 people with severe dandruff or seborrhoeic dermatitis: after 4 weeks, zinc pyrithione 1% improved severity scores by 67% and ketoconazole 2% by 73%; ketoconazole also had fewer relapses. Both were well tolerated.
